text: The standards library | How work is done, everywhere. The fold, the sequence, the thirty-second rule, the food safety floors. Written once, applies in every household, updated centrally.
The household Playbook | This home only. Its preferences, its people, its deviations from the standard. It never repeats what the standards already say.
The Playbook decides everything about this house. It cannot decide anything that would put a person at risk or breach a confidence, because those are not the client’s to give away.
1 | Safety and law | Floors. A household may ask for more caution, never less.
2 | Confidentiality and access | Floors. These protect people who are not in the room.
3 | Well Kept process | The SOP. Client preference does not govern how the company operates.
4 | Method | The standard, unless the Playbook records a deviation.
5 | This house | The Playbook. Its people, its preferences, its facts. Always.
Follow the floor. Do the task the safe way, or do not do it.
Tell the client at the time, warmly and without drama. "I have done it this way because it is a standard we hold in every home. I wanted you to hear it from me rather than notice it later."
Log it in the visit report the same day, marked as a floor conflict.
The CEO owns the client conversation within one business day.
You are never the person who has to win this argument. Raising it is where your part ends.
If something you notice would take less than thirty seconds to put right, put it right now. Do not add it to a list, do not route it, do not save it for next week.
It never applies to anything on the never-touch list in Section 5.
It never authorizes changing a system. Straightening what exists is inside the rule; deciding where something should live is not.
It never applies to anything you are unsure about. Uncertainty makes it a notice-and-ask, however quick it would have been.
It is not a license to do unscoped work. Thirty seconds is thirty seconds, not a quarter of an hour that felt short.
1 | Read first | Playbook notes for this room, caution flags, anything logged last visit. Before touching anything.
2 | Look before you work | Stand in the doorway and take the room in. What changed since last week is the most useful information you will get all visit.
3 | Clear, then clean | Nothing gets cleaned around. Surfaces are cleared first, cleaned second, and reset third.
4 | Top to bottom | Dust and debris fall. Working upward means cleaning the same surface twice.
5 | Dry before wet | Dust and vacuum before anything damp. Water on dust makes mud, on every surface, every time.
6 | Clean toward dirty | Work from the cleanest area to the dirtiest and never back. Cloths and water move one direction only.
7 | Floor last | Always. Then leave, working backward toward the door so you do not walk across what you just finished.
8 | Check from the doorway | Look at the room the way the family will see it, from where they enter. Faults are visible from there that are invisible up close.
Bath towels, for a shelf: in thirds lengthwise, then in half, then in half again. Folded edge faces out, so the shelf shows a clean line rather than a row of hems.
Bath towels, for a rail: in half lengthwise, then draped in thirds over the rail, edges level.
Hand towels: in thirds lengthwise, then in half. Folded edge out.
Washcloths: in quarters, stacked square.
Flat sheets: in half lengthwise twice, then in thirds.
Fitted sheets: corners tucked into corners to square the sheet, then folded as a flat sheet. A fitted sheet folded properly is one of the more visible signs of a trained hand.
Sheet sets: the whole set stored inside one of its own pillowcases, so a set never has to be reassembled from a shelf.
Duvet covers and blankets: in half twice, then in thirds, to the depth of the shelf they live on.

The default is vertical. Folded to a size that stands on its own edge in the drawer, arranged so every item is visible at once. Stacking hides everything below the top item, which is why the bottom of a stack never gets worn.
Shirts and tops: sides folded in, sleeves back, then folded in thirds to stand.
Trousers and jeans: in half lengthwise, then in thirds.
Socks: paired and folded, never balled. Balling stretches the elastic and shortens the life of the pair.
Anything that creases: hung rather than folded, regardless of where it was found.
Personal correspondence, paperwork, documents and screens. Not opened, not read, not sorted by content, not photographed.
Anything in a room, cupboard, drawer or container documented as off-limits. An off-limits space is a confirmed fact about the household, not an oversight.
Medications, beyond moving them to their documented secure place unopened.
Anything that appears to be private, sensitive, or none of your business. If noticing it felt uncomfortable, that is the signal.
Firearms, cash, jewelry and valuables. Do not move, handle, count, or tidy them. Note the location once in the Playbook if it is a safety matter and otherwise leave it entirely alone.
Anything you cannot identify or are not sure is safe to move.

What you see in a home stays in the home. Not repeated to another client, not to a colleague without an operational reason, not to your own household, not as an anonymized story. This is a condition of employment and it is the single thing most likely to end one.
Notice. You will see things a family has stopped seeing: the system they have abandoned, the cupboard nobody can close, the subscription nobody uses, the vendor who is competent but wrong for them.
Note. Put it in the report, in plain terms, without judgment. Describe what you observed rather than what you concluded.
Propose. Offer it the same honest, no-pressure way a tier change is offered, including the option of doing nothing. The client decides. Always.

Nothing is ever proposed in proximity to a loss. Where a household is dealing with a death, a suspected job loss, or acute illness or injury, you absorb friction quietly and propose nothing at all. Adjust without being asked, log the changed rhythms, and let the client re-open the conversation when they are ready. This suspends the third step above entirely, and it holds until they raise it. WK-STD-016 Section 2 sets out which events trigger it.
Put things back in the orientation and position you found them. The handle facing the same way, the chair at the same angle, the blind at the same height.
Photograph anything complicated before you move it, particularly on a first visit or in a room you rarely work.
Leave no trace of the work itself. No products left out, no cloths on taps, no cords left plugged in, no bin bags by the door, no equipment in a hallway.
Close what was closed and leave open what was open.
Do not rearrange for the sake of aesthetics. A surface that looks better to you and different to them is a failure, not an improvement.
Use only what is documented for that household and that surface. Where the Playbook is silent on a surface you are unsure about, use the mildest option available and ask.
Never mix products. Never decant into an unlabeled container.
Cloths are separated by area and never cross. Bathroom cloths never touch a kitchen. A cloth that has touched a toilet touches nothing else at all.
Everything cloth leaves with you at the end of the visit and goes to the laundry, rather than being hung to dry for next week.
Test anything new on an inconspicuous area first, every time, however confident you are.
What was done, briefly, and anything not done and why.
What you noticed: wear, changes, anything approaching a problem, anything the family may want to know.
Supplies low and anything discarded.
Anything you moved that they may look for.
Photographs of the done state for the main rooms worked.
Every flag carries a revisit trigger, set at the moment of flagging. A date or a condition. A flag without one is an observation the household now believes is being watched when it is not.
Re-observe every flagged condition at each visit, not only at its revisit date. A flag records a rate of change as much as a state.
Promote anything degrading faster than its flag assumed rather than leaving it to its original timing.
The changes-noticed entry appears every visit, even when the answer is none.
Note it plainly, in the report, without a solution attached.
Propose nothing here. Section 6 governs what happens next, and the bereavement rule in WK-STD-016 suspends proposing entirely at certain times.
Describe the time rather than the mess. "The school bags live upstairs and get carried down every morning" is useful. "The hall is cluttered" is not.
A household that hears its own lost time described accurately usually solves half of it without being asked, which is a better outcome than any proposal.
Only what the Playbook and the consent record permit, and never beyond the boundaries recorded there.
Never a person, never a child, never a screen, never a document, never anything through a window or an open door.
Never anything that identifies the household, including mail, framed photographs, or a house number.
Photographs are for this client and this record. They are never a marketing asset, in any form, with or without consent.
1 | Read | Allergen record, caution flags, and this week’s notes. Before you touch anything, not when you need it.
2 | Perishables | Groceries on the counter, anything left out, anything thawing. The clock is already running on these and nothing else in the kitchen is time-critical.
3 | Dishes and sink | Everything else needs the sink empty and the counter clear. Do this before you need the space, not after.
4 | Food handling | Produce processed, leftovers portioned and labeled, refrigerator rotated front to back.
5 | Surfaces | Counters, stovetop, backsplash, then the sink itself last so it takes the run-off from everything above.
6 | Appliances | Exteriors every visit, interiors on the cadence in Section 6.
7 | Floor | Always last. Everything above sheds onto it.
8 | Note and report | Lows for the list, anything discarded, anything noticed. Photograph the done state.
Sink empty, dry, and wiped down, including the tap and the drain rim.
Dishwasher either running or emptied. Never left full and idle.
Counters clear of anything that has a home, and wiped, including under anything you moved and put back.
Stovetop clean, including the grates, the knobs, and the ring where a pot has boiled over.
No food left out that should not be. No open packet, no unlabeled container, no thawing item.
Bin emptied if it is more than two-thirds full, and a fresh liner in. Recycling and compost separated as the household documents.
Tea towels and cloths taken to the laundry, a clean one hung.
Floor swept or vacuumed, and mopped on the documented cadence.
The small things put back the way the family has them. The knife block orientation, the fruit bowl position, the chair pushed in.

The last one matters more than it looks. A family notices that their kitchen feels like theirs long before they notice that it is clean. Leaving a room technically finished but subtly rearranged is the most common way a good visit still lands wrong.

Counter, never refrigerated | Tomatoes, basil, bananas, potatoes, onions, garlic, winter squash, whole uncut melon, bread. Refrigeration destroys the texture of tomatoes and turns potato starch to sugar.
Ripen out, then refrigerate | Avocado, stone fruit, pears, kiwi, mango. Once ripe, the fridge buys several more days.
Refrigerate from the start | Berries, leafy greens, broccoli, carrots, celery, grapes, apples, citrus, mushrooms, and anything already cut.

Keep apart | Apples, bananas, avocados, tomatoes, stone fruit and melon all give off ethylene, which ripens and then spoils anything stored beside them. Keep them away from leafy greens, broccoli, carrots, cucumbers and berries. Onions and potatoes stored together ruin both.
Soft herbs, meaning parsley, coriander, dill and mint: trim the stems, stand in a jar of water, loose bag over the top, in the refrigerator. Change the water every two days.
Basil: the same treatment but on the counter, never the refrigerator, which blackens it within a day.
Hardy herbs, meaning rosemary, thyme and sage: wrapped in a barely damp cloth inside a bag, in the refrigerator.
Wash before cutting, including melon, citrus and anything with an inedible rind. The knife carries whatever is on the skin straight through into the flesh.
Do not wash berries or mushrooms until the moment they are used. Both absorb water and spoil faster wet.
Dry leafy greens thoroughly. Water left on them is what turns a bag of salad to slime in two days.

For children under four, the cutting rules in WK-STD-002 Section 7 override every preference and every convenience. Round firm foods are quartered lengthwise, never served whole and never cut into rounds.
Top shelf | Leftovers, ready-to-eat food, drinks. The most temperature-stable shelf.
Middle shelves | Dairy and eggs. Eggs go in the body of the fridge, never in the door.
Bottom shelf | Raw protein, always, on a tray. Coldest shelf, and nothing ready-to-eat ever sits beneath it.
Crispers | High humidity for leafy greens and anything that wilts. Low humidity for fruit and anything that rots.
Door | Condiments only. It is the warmest part and swings most every time the door opens. Never milk, never eggs.
Everything labeled with contents and the date it went in. An unlabeled freezer bag is a future bin item.
Flat-frozen where the shape allows, which stacks better and thaws faster and more evenly.
Air pressed out before sealing. Freezer burn is dehydration, not cold damage.
Raw protein on the lowest level here too, for the same reason as the refrigerator, since a leaking bag does not know what appliance it is in.

Cast iron, carbon steel, seasoned woks | Hot water and a brush or chain scrubber. No soaking, no dishwasher, and no soap unless the Playbook records that this household uses it. Dry on the heat, then a thin wipe of oil. A rusted heirloom pan is not a recoverable mistake.
Nonstick | Cool before washing, since thermal shock warps the base. Hand wash, soft side of the sponge, no metal and no abrasive. Never stack without a liner between.
Stainless steel | Dishwasher safe. For heat discoloration or burnt-on residue use a non-scratch powder cleanser, always with the grain.
Enamelled cast iron | Hand wash, nothing abrasive, no metal utensils. Chipped enamel is permanent.
Wooden boards and utensils | Hand wash, never soak, never in the dishwasher, dry standing on edge. Food-grade mineral oil monthly.

Knives | Hand wash and dry immediately. Never left in the sink under water, which is both how knives are damaged and how people are cut reaching in. Never the dishwasher. Back into the block or on the magnet the same way the household keeps them.
Aluminum and sheet pans | Hand wash. The dishwasher oxidizes aluminum and dulls it permanently.
Stone, marble, butcher block counters | No acid, no vinegar, no citrus cleaner on stone. Use only what the household documents in Playbook Section 13.
Scrape, do not rinse. Modern detergent needs some soil to work against, and pre-rinsing makes the wash less effective, not more.
Everything faces the center and down. Nothing blocks the spray arm, and no large item shelters a small one.
Run it full. A half load run daily costs a family more than it saves in convenience.
Clean the filter monthly. It is the single most neglected part of the machine and the reason most dishwashers stop washing well.
Every visit | Exteriors of all appliances, cooktop, microwave interior, sink and tap, coffee area, and the handles and touch points that everyone forgets.
Weekly | Refrigerator shelf check with expired items pulled, microwave interior properly rather than wiped, sink drain and disposal flushed, bin cleaned rather than just emptied.

Monthly | Refrigerator interior turned out and cleaned, oven interior checked and cleaned if needed, dishwasher filter, kettle and coffee machine descaled per the manufacturer, small appliance interiors including the toaster crumb tray, wooden items oiled.
Quarterly | Refrigerator coils vacuumed, freezer defrost checked, range hood filter cleaned or replaced, water filter changed against the appliance registry, and cabinet interiors and tops wiped.

section_title: What you never do in a client kitchen
text: Prepare or handle any food without reading the allergen record first.

section_title: What you never do in a client kitchen
text: Reorganize a system the household is already running. Notice it, note it, propose it. Weekly service maintains systems and does not replace them.

section_title: What you never do in a client kitchen
text: Introduce new containers or a new labeling scheme. That is the reset service and the container standard, not a weekly visit.

section_title: What you never do in a client kitchen
text: Use a cleaning product that is not documented for that household and that surface.

section_title: What you never do in a client kitchen
text: Discard anything outside the rules in WK-STD-002 Section 8. Set it aside, note it, ask.

section_title: What you never do in a client kitchen
text: Deviate from documented kosher or halal separation, or use a pan, board or sink you are not certain is the right one.

section_title: What you never do in a client kitchen
text: Open, read, or move personal correspondence or paperwork that has accumulated on a kitchen counter. Stack it neatly in the documented place and leave it.

section_title: What you never do in a client kitchen
text: Taste anything with a utensil that goes back into the food.
Staples running low, before they run out rather than after.
Anything discarded, with what it was and why. Over a few months this shows a family where they are losing money.
Anything approaching its date that they may want to use this week.
Appliance behaviour that has changed. A fridge running warm, a dishwasher not draining, an unfamiliar noise, a seal that no longer seals.
Anything you found that suggests the household is quietly abandoning a system, which is worth naming honestly and without judgment.
A photograph of the done state.

Tier 1 floor under WK-STD-000 Section 1. Everything in this document is a floor. A household may ask for more caution here, never less. If a documented preference would breach a floor, follow the floor and flag it the same day.
Read the allergen record before every food task. Every time, from the document, never from memory. This holds on your two hundredth visit to a household you know well.
Read the label on every product, including familiar ones. Manufacturers reformulate without notice and without changing the packaging.
If a product is unlabeled, decanted, or the label is unreadable, do not use it. Ask.
Treat a "may contain" or shared-line warning as a yes in any household with a documented allergy, unless the Playbook explicitly records that the family accepts it.
Use the dedicated boards, utensils, pans and toaster where the Playbook documents them. Where it does not and a serious allergy exists, wash and dry equipment before use and flag the gap.
Never taste with a utensil that returns to the food, and never share a utensil between an allergen-containing dish and a safe one.
Perishable food out of refrigeration for more than two hours is discarded. If the room is above 90 degrees, the limit is one hour. This is cumulative across the day, not per occasion.
Appliance | Target | Standard
Refrigerator | 40°F or below | Verify with an appliance thermometer monthly. If the household has none, flag it rather than assume the dial is accurate.
Freezer | 0°F or below | Verify monthly. Ice crystals on stored food or a soft texture indicate the unit is running warm.
Hot holding | 140°F or above | Anything held warm for a later meal. Below this, it is cooling and the two-hour clock applies.
Poultry, whole or ground, and any stuffed dish | 165°F | No rest required
Ground beef, pork, lamb, veal | 160°F
Whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, veal | 145°F | Rest three minutes
Fish and shellfish | 145°F | Opaque and flaking
Egg dishes | 160°F | Eggs cooked to order until firm
Anything reheated | 165°F | Throughout, not just at the edge
Divide into shallow containers no more than two inches deep. Depth is what governs cooling speed, not the size of the fridge.
Leave uncovered or loosely covered until cool, then seal. A tight lid on hot food traps heat and steams the contents into the danger zone for longer.
Never put a large hot pot straight into the refrigerator. It raises the temperature of everything around it and puts food you did not cook at risk.
An ice bath, a shallow tray, or dividing into portions all work. Standing on the counter to cool does not.
In the refrigerator. The only method that is safe unattended. Plan a day ahead, on the bottom shelf, on a tray.
In cold running water. Sealed, water below 70 degrees, changed every thirty minutes. Cook immediately afterwards.
In the microwave. Cook immediately afterwards, because parts of the food will already have warmed.

Never on the counter. The outside of the food is in the danger zone for hours before the center thaws. If you find something thawing on a counter, the two-hour rule applies from the moment you found it and you should assume the worst about what came before.
Item | Refrigerated | Note
Cooked leftovers, general | 3 to 4 days | Four days is the absolute ceiling
Cooked rice, pasta, and other cooked grains | 1 day | Shorter than people expect. Cool fast, refrigerate immediately.
Raw poultry and any ground meat | 1 to 2 days | Freeze if not used
Raw whole cuts of meat | 3 to 5 days
Raw fish and shellfish | 1 to 2 days
Deli meat and prepared salads, once opened | 3 to 5 days
Cut fruit and vegetables | 3 to 5 days | Cut produce is ready-to-eat food and carries the same care as cooked food
Soft cheese, opened | 1 week
Eggs in shell | 3 to 5 weeks | Store in the body of the fridge, never the door
Marinating anything | In the fridge | Never on the counter. Discard used marinade unless boiled.

Cooked rice is the one most people get wrong. Bacillus cereus survives cooking and produces a toxin at room temperature that reheating does not destroy. Rice cools fast, refrigerates immediately, and keeps one day.

Raw protein lives on the bottom shelf, always, on a tray or in a sealed container. Nothing ready-to-eat ever sits below it. This is the single most common refrigerator error and the one with the worst consequences.
Use a separate board for raw protein. Where the household has color-coded boards, follow their scheme and record it in the Playbook. Where they do not, use a dedicated board and wash it between uses.
Never return cooked food to the plate, board or container that held it raw.
Never rinse raw poultry. Rinsing does not clean it and it spreads bacteria across the sink, the counter and anything within three feet.
Wash hands, boards, knives and surfaces immediately after any contact with raw protein, before touching anything else.
Keep raw protein sealed and separate in the grocery bag, the refrigerator and on the counter.

Where a household keeps kosher or halal separation, that separation is both a religious obligation and a contamination control. Follow it exactly as documented in Playbook Sections 12 and 16, and if you are unsure which board or which sink, ask rather than guess.
Never use the same cloth on a raw protein surface and then on dishes, a counter, or a table.
Cloths go to the laundry at the end of every visit rather than back on the tap.
Sponges are replaced on the cadence documented for the household, and a sponge that smells has already needed replacing for some time.
For children under four, round firm foods are quartered lengthwise, never served whole and never cut into rounds. A round slice is the shape most likely to seal an airway.
Grapes, cherry tomatoes and similar: quartered lengthwise.
Hot dogs and sausages: quartered lengthwise, never sliced into coins.
Raw hard vegetables such as carrot and celery: grated, or cooked until soft. Not sticks or coins.
Whole nuts, popcorn, hard sweets and chunks of raw apple: not served to under-fours at all.
Nut butters: spread thin. Never by the spoonful and never in a thick layer.
Honey: never to a child under twelve months, in any form, including baked into something.
Children sit down to eat. Not walking, not playing, not in a car seat, and never unattended.
Anything past its use-by date.
Anything that has breached the two-hour rule or that you found out of refrigeration with no way to know how long.
Anything visibly spoiled, moldy, or in a swollen, leaking or damaged container.
Anything reheated and not eaten.
Anything unlabeled in a refrigerator where labeling is our standard and you cannot establish its age.
If there is any sign of a reaction or illness, call emergency services first. Do not wait to reach the client.
Tell the client immediately, the same hour, whatever the circumstances and whoever was at fault.
Tell your Well Kept contact the same day.
Keep the food, the packaging and the container. Do not clean up the evidence of what happened.
Write it down while it is fresh: what, when, quantity, who, and what you observed.

Reporting an error you made will never cost you your job at Well Kept. Concealing one will. We can manage almost anything a family experiences if we know about it within the hour, and very little of it if we find out a week later.
Treat this space as a corridor, not a closet. The measure of a good entryway is not how much it holds. It is how little stays.

Follow the household’s shoe practice from your first step inside. Where a home is shoes-off, carry dedicated indoor shoes or covers and change at the door every time, including on a two-minute drop-in.
Your coat, bag and keys go in one documented place, out of the family’s flow. Never on a bench, hook or counter that belongs to them.
In wet or snowy weather, deal with your own footwear before you walk anywhere. Tracked-in salt and water is the most common way a House Manager creates work rather than removing it.
Handle the alarm exactly as the Playbook documents, including the quirks. Never prop an exterior door open while you carry things in, even for a moment.
Leave through this room last. It is the final space you reset, after everything else is done, because everything you carry out passes through it.
The path from the door into the house is completely clear. Not narrowed, not stepped around. Clear.
Floor swept or vacuumed, dry, and mopped on the documented cadence. Mats shaken or vacuumed on both sides, and the floor underneath them cleaned too.
Every pair of shoes in its documented place. No loose pairs, no single shoes, nothing under a bench.
Coats hung rather than draped. Bags on hooks or in their documented spots rather than on the floor.
Inbound zone empty. Everything that arrived has traveled to where it belongs.
Outbound zone staged and ready to leave in one motion.
Surfaces clear and wiped, including the bench, the console, and the top of anything.
Nothing homeless left sitting out. Anything without a home is in the documented landing spot and logged.
Exterior door glass and handles wiped, and the outside step swept where it is in scope.
Inbound | What has just arrived and needs to travel further in. Mail, packages, groceries, dry cleaning, school paperwork. This zone should be empty when you leave, every visit, without exception.

Outbound | What is leaving. Returns, dry cleaning, library books, donations, the sports bag for tomorrow, the forms that need to reach school. Staged so it can be picked up in one motion on the way out.
Transit | The only permanent residents. Shoes, coats, bags, keys, umbrellas, leashes. Everything here goes in and out daily, and anything that has not moved in a month is not really transit.
Follow the household’s documented shoe practice exactly, including how it applies to guests and to contractors.
In wet weather, wet items are separated so they actually dry rather than stacked so they stay damp. Boots on a tray, upside down or on a boot rack, never toe-to-toe in a wet pile.

Winter salt and grit damages hardwood, stone and finished concrete. Clear it promptly, and clean it off the floor rather than sweeping it around. Note recurring damage to the client rather than letting it accumulate quietly.
A wet floor in the highest-traffic doorway in the house is a real fall risk. Dry it rather than leaving it to air, especially where anyone in the household is elderly or unsteady.
Check mat backing for slip and curl every visit. A rucked mat in a doorway causes more falls than a wet floor does.
Never open or read personal correspondence. Sort it to the documented place and leave it. This holds regardless of how obvious the contents seem or how helpful opening it would be.

Anything perishable or temperature-sensitive first. Grocery deliveries, meal kits, refrigerated medication and anything marked as such go in before anything else in the visit begins. A delivery sitting at the door is already on the clock, and WK-STD-002 Section 3 applies from the moment it was left, not from the moment you found it.
Medication next, to the documented secure location. Never left in an entryway, and never in reach of a child or a pet.
Then everything else, brought fully inside rather than left inside the door.
Bring in anything left outside, including anything at a side or back door, and check for deliveries the household may not know arrived.
Open, unbox or leave sealed exactly as the Playbook documents. Where it is silent, leave sealed.
Break down and flatten boxes and put them out with recycling. Do not leave large boxes advertising an expensive purchase at the curb, which is a security matter as much as a tidiness one.
Photograph the delivery where the household documents that preference, taking care that the photograph does not show the interior of the home through an open door.
Move it to the documented landing spot for unhomed items and note it in the report.

If the same item or the same category appears three visits running, that is a systems signal rather than a tidiness one. Name it plainly: this household has nowhere for its reusable bags, or its sunglasses, or its charging cables.

Repeated accumulation in this room is one of the clearest indicators that a Focused Reset of the entryway would earn its cost. Flag it and propose it the same honest, no-pressure way any recommendation is made. The client decides.
Out-of-season outerwear, footwear and gear stored per the Playbook. In-season items accessible at the height the person using them can reach.
Size children’s outerwear and boots before the season, not during it. Checking in September whether last year’s snow boots still fit is worth more than any other single task this room generates.

Children’s shoes run on their own quarterly cadence, separate from the seasonal check. Feet outgrow shoes faster than bodies outgrow clothes, the consequence is pain and blisters rather than an unflattering hem, and children frequently do not report it.
Rotate what belongs: umbrellas and rain gear in spring, sun hats and water bottles in summer, sports equipment against the season on the calendar, snow gear and salt before the first forecast.
Note what did not survive storage and what will need replacing, early enough that the family can buy it without paying for urgency.
Keys and codes are never labeled with a client’s name or address, anywhere, including in your own belongings and your own phone.
Never leave a key in a lock, under a mat, or in any external hiding place, and never write a code down within the space it opens.

Arm and disarm exactly as documented, including the quirks. If the alarm behaves differently from the record, flag it the same day, because a system behaving unexpectedly is a system nobody can rely on.
Follow the household’s door-answering policy exactly: whether you open the door at all, and for whom.
Never grant access to anyone not documented without real-time client approval. Not a contractor who says they are expected, not a delivery driver who wants to come in, not a neighbor.
Never prop an exterior door, and never leave the house unlocked while you work elsewhere in it.
Report a failed exterior light, a lock that has begun sticking, or a door that no longer seats properly on the day you notice it. These are security findings, not maintenance notes.

The path to every exterior door stays clear at all times. This is a fire egress requirement rather than a tidiness preference, and it holds even mid-task. Never stage a pile of anything across an exit.
No cords, cables or charger leads across a walkway.
In households with a child under five, confirm the door security the family uses is engaged when you leave the room. The entry is where small children bolt, and it happens fast and silently.
In households with a dog, the same applies. Know the household’s door protocol before you open anything, and know where the leash lives.

Check that smoke and carbon monoxide detectors in or near this space are present and functioning as part of the sentinel sweep, since the entry hall is where they are most often located and most often ignored.
Open, read or move personal correspondence beyond sorting it to its documented place.
Discard anything that arrived, including packaging, before confirming the household does not need it. Shipping labels and packing slips are often needed for returns.
Reorganize the household’s existing entry system. Notice, note, propose.
Introduce new hooks, bins, baskets or labels. That belongs to the reset service and the container standard, not to a weekly visit.
Move or handle anything in a documented off-limits closet or cupboard that happens to open into this space.
Leave the outbound zone staged with anything perishable, or with anything that should not sit in an unheated or unconditioned space.
Deliveries received, including anything found outside and how long it may have been there.
Returns processed and returns approaching their deadline.
Items with no home, and any pattern across recent visits.
Anything that will need replacing before the next season, early enough to buy calmly.
Security findings: lighting, locks, doors, alarm behavior, anything that did not match the record.
Wear the family may not have noticed, since this floor and these fittings take more traffic than anything else in the house.
A photograph of the done state, taken from inside looking toward the door, so the cleared path is visible.
1 | Clear and ventilate | Personal items off surfaces to one spot, extractor on or window open. Products need air and so does the room.

2 | Apply and wait | Product into the toilet bowl and onto shower and tub surfaces first, then leave it to work while you do everything else. Dwell time does the cleaning; scrubbing is what you do when you did not wait.
3 | Dust and high surfaces | Light fittings, extractor vent, tops of frames and cabinets, corners.
4 | Mirrors and glass | Before anything wet happens near them.
5 | Sink, counter, fittings | Including the tap base, the overflow, the plughole and the underside of the spout.
6 | Shower and tub | Return to what has been dwelling. Rinse fully, then dry the glass and fittings.
7 | Toilet | Last, with dedicated cloths that touch nothing else, ever. Bowl, seat both sides, hinges, base, the floor behind and around it.
8 | Restock and reset | Towels, paper, supplies. Personal items back exactly where they were.
9 | Floor, then out | Backing toward the door. Leave the extractor running if the household does.

In a multi-bathroom home, walk them all first and apply product in every one before working any of them. The dwell time then runs in four rooms at once instead of four times in a row, which is usually twenty minutes of a visit. Fresh cloths per room still applies, per Section 4.
Every surface dry. Not clean-and-damp. A bathroom left wet is a bathroom that will show water spots within the hour and grow something within the week.
Mirrors and glass streak-free, checked from an angle and not straight on, which is the only way streaks are visible.
Chrome and metal fittings dry and buffed, with no water spotting at the tap base.
Toilet clean including the hinges, the base, and the floor behind it. These are the three places that get missed and the three a family checks.
Towels hung or changed per the documented cadence, edges level, folded to the standard in WK-STD-000.
Paper stocked, with a spare visible or in the documented place.
Personal items back in their exact positions.
Bin emptied and liner replaced. No exceptions and no judgment about contents.
Floor clean and dry, including behind the door and around the pedestal or vanity base.
The room smells of nothing. Not of product, and not of scent added to cover something.

Natural stone: marble, travertine, limestone | No acid, ever. No vinegar, no citrus, no lime scale remover, no bathroom cleaner unless it is explicitly stone-safe. Acid etches stone permanently in seconds and the damage cannot be polished out on site.
Grout | Soft brush, never a wire or hard-bristle brush. Note discoloration and failing grout rather than attacking it, since grout that has gone is a repair rather than a cleaning problem.
Glass shower screens | Squeegee then dry. The reason screens cloud permanently is minerals left to dry on them, so drying matters more than the product used.
Brushed and matte finishes | Always with the grain, never abrasive. A circular wipe on brushed metal leaves marks that do not come out.
Mirrors | Never spray directly onto the glass. Liquid runs into the bottom edge and destroys the silvering from behind. Onto the cloth, then onto the mirror.
Wood vanities and cabinetry | Damp not wet, dried immediately. Standing water at the base of a vanity is how the panel swells.
A cloth that has touched a toilet touches nothing else. Not the floor, not the sink, not another bathroom, not a rinse in between. It goes straight into the bag to be laundered.
Cloths are separated by zone: mirrors and glass, sinks and counters, shower and tub, toilet, floor. Five, and they do not cross.
Where a household provides color-coded cloths, follow their scheme and record it in the Playbook.
Bathroom cloths never enter a kitchen, in any circumstance.
Every cloth used leaves with you at the end of the visit. Nothing is rinsed and rehung for next week.
In a multi-bathroom home, do not carry a used set from one bathroom to the next. Fresh cloths per room.
Wash hands between bathrooms and after the toilet stage, every time.
Change on the documented cadence rather than on appearance. A towel that looks fine has usually been in use for longer than the household would choose.

Where no cadence is documented, propose one rather than assuming. Bath towels twice weekly and hand towels every visit is the standing default. Adopted as a pilot default rather than a settled standard, and reviewed at pilot close against what households actually chose.
Hung to the standard in WK-STD-000, edges level, spread rather than bunched so they actually dry.
Bath mats hung to dry rather than left flat on the floor, which is where the smell comes from.
Note anything worn, thin, or fraying in the report. Towels wear out invisibly and families replace them years later than they would like to.
Under the sink, every visit. A damp spot, a swollen cabinet base, a cupped or lifting floor panel, or a musty smell in a closed cupboard.
Around the toilet base and behind it, for damp or staining.
The seal where the tub or shower meets the wall and floor, for gaps, lifting, or blackening.
A toilet that continues running after it fills, which is both a water bill and a failing part.
Slow drains, which are a warning rather than an inconvenience.
The extractor fan actually pulling. Hold a square of paper to it. A fan that runs but does not pull is the most common cause of a mold problem nobody can find the source of.
Ceiling and upper wall corners for the first shadow of mold, which appears there before anywhere else.
Do not open a medicine cabinet or a closed drawer unless the Playbook documents that you clean inside it.

Do not read labels on medication, and do not inventory, count, move or mention it. If a medication is somewhere it should not be for a child’s safety, that is the one exception and it goes to the client directly and privately.
Do not examine, comment on, or reposition personal items beyond moving them to clean and putting them back exactly.
Do not photograph any bathroom surface holding personal items, in any report, ever.
Empty the bin without looking in it, and never remark on anything it contained.

What you notice in a bathroom does not go in a report, does not go to a colleague, and does not go anywhere else. Health information seen incidentally is held in exactly the same confidence as everything else.

Check that anything hazardous is stored where the household documents. Cleaning products, medication, razors and small items belong out of reach in a home with young children, and finding one within reach is a same-day flag rather than a report line.
Bath toys hold water and grow mold internally. Drain, dry, and note any that need replacing.
Non-slip mats and treads checked for lifting or wear.
Step stools clean, stable, and back where the child can reach them.
Guest bathrooms are left guest-ready every visit regardless of use: fresh towels, paper stocked, a light clean, and nothing personal left out.
Use acid on stone, or any product not documented for that surface.
Mix products. Bleach and ammonia together produce chlorine gas, and several common bathroom cleaners contain one or the other.
Work without ventilation.
Move or reorganize the contents of a cabinet, a drawer, or a shower caddy.
Discard anything, including something that appears empty or expired. Note it and ask.
Everything from the sentinel check in Section 6, described plainly and without diagnosis. Report the damp spot, not the plumbing theory.
Grout, seal and caulk condition, tracked over time so the household sees it change.
Towels and mats needing replacement.
Anything a repair visit would be cheaper to do now than later, which in this room is nearly everything.
A photograph of the done state, framed to include no personal items.
Read first. Room notes, caution flags, whose room this is and what they have asked for.
Strip or straighten. Linens off if it is a change day, bed pulled back to air if it is not.
Clear surfaces. Only what has a documented home. Everything else stays where it is.
Dust top to bottom. Fittings, frames, headboard, shelves, sills, skirting.
Make the bed. After dusting, before floors, since bed-making sheds.
Reset surfaces. Everything back exactly, in the same orientation.
Floors last, including under the bed where access allows, backing out toward the door.
Fitted sheet square and taut, corners fully seated, no rucking at the foot.
Flat sheet, where used, patterned side down so it shows correctly when the top is turned back.
Hospital corners at the foot unless the household prefers otherwise.
Duvet or cover shaken out and settled evenly, corners filled, no cold spot at the foot.
Pillows plumped and standing, in the household’s own arrangement and order. Note which pillow belongs to which side, because people are particular about this and rarely say so.
Turn-down where the household documents it, and never where they do not.

Changed on the documented cadence, not on appearance. Where nothing is documented, weekly for primary beds is the standing default. Adopted as a pilot default rather than a settled standard, and reviewed at pilot close.
Rotate through the household’s sets rather than washing and returning the same set, so wear spreads evenly.
Sets stored together inside one of their own pillowcases, folded to the standard in WK-STD-000.
Mattress protectors checked and laundered on their own cadence. They are usually forgotten entirely.
Note thinning, pilling, or elastic that has gone. Households replace linens years later than they would choose to, purely because nobody tracks it.
Move only what you must to clean, and return it to the same position and orientation. Photograph it first if it is complicated.
Do not open a nightstand drawer unless the Playbook documents that you clean inside it.
Do not stack, square up, or tidy papers, books, or personal items into an arrangement they were not in.
Charging cables coiled and returned, never unplugged from a device that was charging.
Water glasses and dishes taken to the kitchen unless the household prefers otherwise.
Do not read anything. Not a note, not a book’s open page, not a screen that wakes when you move it.

Weekly service maintains a closet. It does not reorganize one. Rehanging what has slipped, straightening what has tipped, and returning what has migrated is maintenance. Deciding where things should go is a reset, and a reset is a separate scoped conversation.

Return laundered items to their own place, hung or folded to the household’s existing scheme. If you cannot tell where something goes, it goes to the documented landing spot and into the report rather than a reasonable guess.
Hangers facing one direction, matched where the household uses matching hangers, and spaced so garments are not crushed.
Anything that creases hangs, whatever state you found it in.
Shoes paired and in their documented place.
Note anything needing repair, cleaning, or return: a fallen hem, a missing button, a dry-clean-only item in the wash pile, something still tagged.

Garment condition is noticed. Adult body size is never observed. For children, checking fit is straightforward anticipatory care. For adults it is not: bodies change for reasons that are private, sometimes medical and sometimes painful, and assessing whether an adult’s clothes still fit crosses from service into scrutiny. Adult sizing is owner-initiated only, asked rather than looked at, and acted on when a household member raises it.
Do not open a closed drawer that is not documented as yours to work in.
Under-bed storage is left alone unless documented. It is where households keep the things they least want handled.

Small parts, batteries, magnets and anything a younger sibling could reach are the first thing to check and a same-day flag rather than a report line. Button batteries in particular are a medical emergency if swallowed, not a choking risk in the ordinary sense.
Cords, blind pulls and cables kept off cots and out of reach.
Anything a child can climb checked for tipping. Furniture anchoring is worth noting if it is absent.
Toys returned to the household’s existing system, not to a better one. A child needs to find things where the child expects them.
Note outgrown clothing and shoes as you handle them. This is one of the most useful things this room generates, because families discover outgrown shoes at the worst possible moment.
Schoolwork, drawings and anything made by the child is never discarded, moved out of sight, or tidied into a bin. Ever. To an adult it is clutter and to a child it is not.
Bedding for younger children changed more often than the adult cadence, and immediately after illness.
Read nothing. Not correspondence, not a journal, not a screen, not a note on a pillow.
Open nothing that is not documented as yours to open.
Handle nothing in the categories in WK-STD-000 Section 5: medication, cash, jewelry, valuables, firearms, or anything that feels private.
Photograph no bedroom surface holding personal items, and no bedroom at all where the Playbook has not recorded consent.
Notice nothing out loud. What you see in a bedroom is not mentioned to the client, to a colleague, or to anyone, and does not appear in a report unless it is a safety matter.
If you find something you were not meant to see, put it back as it was, say nothing, and carry on. That is the whole procedure.
Reorganize a closet, a drawer, or a surface.
Discard anything at all, including something that appears to be trash. Bedrooms are where discarded-by-mistake becomes a serious problem.
Move a personal item you are unsure about, even to clean under it. Clean around it and note it.
Change bedding on a bed you were not asked to, or in a room documented as off-limits.
Work in an adult’s bedroom when that adult is in it, unless they have invited you to. Come back later.
Use scent, spray, or anything fragranced unless the household documents it. Bedrooms are where sensitivity to this is highest.
Linens changed and which set is in use.
Anything needing repair, cleaning, or return.
Outgrown clothing and shoes, with enough notice to replace them calmly.
Wear on mattresses, linens, and window coverings.
Safety findings in children’s rooms, and anything flagged same-day rather than held for the report.
Anything you moved that they may look for.
Photographs only of the made bed and general condition, framed to include nothing personal.
Almost every serious laundry error is a heat error. When you are unsure about anything, choose colder, gentler and slower. Nothing is ever ruined by being washed too carefully.

section_title: The sequence, and why it is not linear
text: Laundry is the only work in the house where a machine does the waiting for you, which makes the washer the constraint on the whole visit. Every minute it sits idle is a minute you cannot get back. A visit that follows one load from beginning to end produces one load. A visit that keeps the machine loaded produces three.

section_title: The sequence, and why it is not linear
text: Collect. Every documented hamper, every visit, including the ones people forget: the gym bag, the car, the mud room, the towels in the guest bath nobody used.

section_title: The sequence, and why it is not linear
text: Empty pockets and check. Before sorting, not after. Pens, lipsticks, tissues and phones cost more to fix than the entire visit.

section_title: The sequence, and why it is not linear
text: Inspect for stains and damage. The step that gets skipped and the one that matters most, because a stain that goes through a dryer is a stain forever.

section_title: The sequence, and why it is not linear
text: Sort the whole collection, not the first load. Sorting once is faster than sorting three times, and it tells you how many loads this visit needs, which is what the rest of the visit gets planned around.

section_title: The sequence, and why it is not linear
text: Treat stains across every pile, not just the one going in now. Treatment works better with time on it anyway.

section_title: The sequence, and why it is not linear
text: Load one in, and leave the room. Nothing else in the laundry is time-critical and everything else in the house can wait ten minutes.

section_title: The sequence, and why it is not linear
text: Return to the machine on its schedule, not when you happen to finish something else. A load left sitting wet is time you cannot recover and a smell you will have to wash out.

section_title: The sequence, and why it is not linear
text: One trip does both ends. Wash out to the dryer and the next load in, in the same visit to the room. Never two trips for one handover.

section_title: The sequence, and why it is not linear
text: Check every treated item before it goes near the dryer, every time. If the stain is still there, it does not go in.

section_title: The sequence, and why it is not linear
text: Hang-dry items come out first and go up immediately, so they have the whole visit to dry rather than the last twenty minutes of it.

section_title: The sequence, and why it is not linear
text: Fold while a cycle runs. Folding is the only laundry task that needs no machine, no water and no waiting, which makes it the right thing to be doing whenever you are waiting for anything else in the house.

section_title: The sequence, and why it is not linear
text: Work back from when you leave. The last load goes in early enough to finish. If it will not finish, it does not start, and you say so in the report rather than leaving it wet for the household to find.

section_title: The sequence, and why it is not linear
text: Put away, folded to the standard in WK-STD-000, into each item’s own place.

section_title: The sequence, and why it is not linear
text: Reset the room. Lint trap, surfaces, machine doors left ajar, floor.
Color. Whites, lights, darks, and anything new or intensely dyed washed separately the first two or three times.
Fabric weight and type. Heavy cottons abrade delicates. Towels and lint-shedding items never go with anything dark or smooth.
Soil level. Heavily soiled items washed separately rather than redistributing soil across a full load.
Care requirement. Anything requiring cold, delicate, or hand washing comes out and goes in its own load, however small.
Temperature | Use for | Note
Cold | Most things | The default. Preserves color, prevents shrinkage, and is the only safe choice for any protein stain. Modern detergents work at cold.
Warm | Everyday cottons, moderate soil | A reasonable middle where a household wants more cleaning power.
Hot | Sanitizing only | Bed linens after illness, kitchen cloths, cleaning cloths. It shrinks, fades, and permanently sets protein stains. Never a default and never on anything unfamiliar.

Under-dose rather than over-dose. Most households use two to four times what is needed. Excess detergent does not rinse out. It leaves residue that stiffens fabric, irritates skin, holds odor, and builds up inside the machine.
Use the household’s documented product. Where anyone in the home has sensitive skin, eczema, or a young baby, fragrance-free is the default unless the Playbook says otherwise.
High-efficiency machines take HE detergent only. Ordinary detergent over-foams and leaves residue on every load afterward.

Never put a stained item in the dryer. Heat sets a stain permanently and no later treatment will lift it. If the stain survived the wash, it goes back for a second treatment, air dries, or waits for the client. This is the single most important rule in this document.
Act as soon as you find it. Almost every stain is removable when fresh and permanent when old.
Blot, never rub. Rubbing drives the stain deeper into the fiber and damages the weave.
Work from the outside of the stain inward, so you do not spread the ring.
Test any treatment on an inside seam first, every time.
Stain type | Water | Approach
Protein: blood, dairy, egg, sweat, vomit | Cold only | Warm water cooks protein into the fiber and the stain becomes permanent. Rinse cold, then an enzyme treatment.
Oil and grease | Warm | Absorb excess first, then a degreasing treatment worked in before washing.
Tannin: wine, coffee, tea, fruit juice | Cold | Flush from the back of the fabric to push the stain out rather than through. Never soap first, which can set some tannins.
Ink, marker, cosmetics | Cold | Solvent based. Blot from behind onto a clean cloth so the stain transfers out. Change the cloth constantly.
Mud and dirt | Cold | Let it dry completely, then brush off the solid before any water touches it. Wet mud spreads.
Unknown | Cold | Cold water, gentle treatment, air dry, and flag it. Never guess with heat.
Clean the lint trap before every single load. Not daily, not weekly. Every load. Lint is the leading cause of dryer fires and a blocked trap also doubles drying time.
Do not overload. Air has to move for anything to dry, and a packed drum creases everything.
Remove promptly and fold or hang immediately. Most of what gets ironed only needs ironing because it sat in a warm drum.
Hang rather than tumble: anything wool or cashmere, anything with elastane or spandex, athletic and technical fabrics, silk, linen, bras, swimwear, and anything you are unsure about.
Dry flat on a towel, reshaped by hand: knitwear, wool, cashmere. Hanging a wet sweater stretches it out of shape permanently.
Down and feather items need thorough drying with dryer balls to break up clumps. Down that is put away slightly damp will mildew from the inside and cannot be recovered.
Never tumble anything flame-resistant, rubber-backed, or with printed graphics on high heat.
Wool and cashmere | Cold, wool cycle or hand wash, wool-specific detergent. Never wrung or twisted. Pressed between towels, then dried flat and reshaped.
Silk | Hand wash or the gentlest cycle in a mesh bag, cold, pH-neutral detergent. No chlorine bleach, no wringing, no direct sun. Many silks are dry clean only and the label decides.
Athletic and technical | Cold, inside out, no softener, no high heat. Heat destroys elastane and softener blocks the wicking that the fabric exists for.
Bras and delicates | Hooks fastened, mesh bag, cold, gentle cycle. Never tumble dried, which is what kills the elastic.
Baby and children | Washed separately where the household documents it, fragrance-free, no softener on sleepwear. Note the flame-resistance rule above.
Down and outerwear | Front-loading machine only, gentle, dried completely with dryer balls. Never dry cleaned unless the label says so.
Anything labeled dry clean only | Does not go in a machine, ever, under any circumstance. Set aside, log it, and route it through the documented service.

section_title: The laundry room as a space
text: Lint trap cleared, and the housing behind it checked periodically for buildup.

section_title: The laundry room as a space
text: Wipe detergent drips and residue from the machine, the dispenser drawer and the surfaces around them. Dried detergent is why a laundry room smells the way it does.

section_title: The laundry room as a space
text: Front-loader door and gasket wiped and dried, and the door left ajar between uses. A sealed wet gasket is where the smell and the black mold come from.

section_title: The laundry room as a space
text: Floor swept and mopped, including behind and between the machines where lint and socks accumulate.

section_title: The laundry room as a space
text: Check the water supply hoses every visit. Look for bulging, cracking, corrosion at the coupling, or any damp. A burst washing machine hose is one of the most expensive and most preventable claims a household will ever make.

section_title: The laundry room as a space
text: Check the floor and wall behind the machines for staining or damp.

section_title: The laundry room as a space
text: Note the dryer vent condition, and flag it for professional cleaning if drying times have lengthened.
Put a stained item in the dryer.
Machine wash anything labeled dry clean only.
Wash a documented specialty or heirloom item against its care instruction, however confident you are.
Mix a household’s delicates into a general load to save time.
Use a product not documented for that household.
Discard anything, including a single sock, an item that seems ruined, or anything found in a pocket. All of it is noted and set aside.
Read anything found in a pocket. Set it aside in the documented place, unread.

Assess whether an adult’s clothes still fit. You handle every garment in the house every week, which makes this the easiest line in the library to cross without meaning to. Garment condition is yours to notice. Adult body size is not. Children’s fit is covered in WK-STD-016 Section 3.
Leave a load in a machine at the end of a visit, wet, to sour before the next one.
Anything treated and anything that did not come out, with what you tried.
Anything needing repair, professional cleaning, or replacement: a hem, a button, a zip, thinning fabric, elastic that has gone.

A narrowing rotation. When the same few items keep cycling through the wash while the rest sit, that is a signal worth raising. The cause may be fit, a garment needing repair, one buried and unseen, or one that was never liked. It prompts a question, never a conclusion.
Anything found in a pocket and where you put it.
Items that are dry clean only and are accumulating.
Everything from the sentinel check: hoses, damp, vent, drying times, machine behavior.

section_title: The four rules that prevent most damage
text: Identify before you clean. If you cannot say what a surface is made of, you cannot know what is safe on it. Marble and quartz look alike and behave completely differently. Ask, or use plain water and note it.

section_title: The four rules that prevent most damage
text: Mildest first. Start with the least aggressive option that could work and escalate only if needed. You can always do more. You cannot undo an etch, a scratch, or a stripped finish.

section_title: The four rules that prevent most damage
text: Test on the inconspicuous. Under a rug edge, behind a door, inside a cabinet. Every new product, every time, however familiar it is.

section_title: The four rules that prevent most damage
text: Damp, never wet, and dry immediately. Standing water is what destroys wood, stone, grout and cabinetry. Almost nothing in a house is improved by more water.

Hardwood, solid or engineered | Vacuum or sweep first, always. Damp mop with a wood-specific cleaner and a well-wrung mop, then dry. Never steam, never wet mop, never vinegar, never oil soap on a polyurethane finish. Water in a seam swells the board and does not go back.
Laminate | Barely damp only. Laminate is paper and resin over fiberboard, and water at a seam causes irreversible swelling at the edges. Never steam.
Luxury vinyl and LVP | The most forgiving floor in most homes. Damp mop, neutral cleaner. Avoid abrasives and solvent-based products, which dull the wear layer.
Ceramic and porcelain tile | Tolerant of most things. The grout is the vulnerable part: soft brush only, and a neutral cleaner rather than anything acidic, which erodes it over time.

Natural stone: marble, limestone, travertine | No acid, ever. No vinegar, no citrus, no bathroom or lime scale product unless it says stone-safe. Acid etches in seconds and the mark is permanent. pH-neutral stone cleaner only, dried immediately.
Granite and slate | More acid-tolerant than marble but still sealed, and the sealant is what fails. Neutral cleaner, no abrasives. Note when water stops beading, which means the seal needs renewing.
Polished or sealed concrete | Neutral cleaner only. Acid and degreasers strip the seal and leave dull patches that cannot be blended.
Cork and bamboo | Barely damp, dried at once, and no standing water at all. Both are more absorbent than they look.
Carpet | Slow passes, several directions. Blot spills, never rub. No heat and no household cleaner on an unknown fiber, and never wet-clean without documented instruction.

Turn the beater bar off for wool, silk, looped pile, sisal, jute and anything antique or hand-knotted. A rotating brush pulls loops, shreds fibers and fuzzes a wool rug permanently. This is the most common way a valuable rug is quietly destroyed over a year of good intentions.
Never vacuum a fringe. Work along it, or brush it by hand in the direction it lies.
Silk and antique rugs are cleaned by a specialist, not by us. Note them in the Playbook so nobody has to decide in the moment.
Rotate rugs on the documented cadence so wear and sun fading spread evenly.
Check rug pads and backing for slip and curl, which is a fall risk as much as a wear one.
Quartz, engineered stone | Neutral cleaner. No abrasives, no bleach, and nothing hot placed directly on it, because the resin binder scorches and the mark is permanent.
Butcher block and wood counters | Damp cloth, dried immediately, never soaked. Food-grade mineral oil on the documented cadence. Never dish soap left standing, which strips the oil.
Wood furniture | Dust dry or barely damp with the grain, dried at once. No silicone polish unless the household uses it, since it builds a film that a refinisher then has to strip.
Stainless steel | Always with the grain, never across it. No chlorine bleach, which pits it. Fingerprints need a dedicated product, not more scrubbing.
Brass, copper and unlacquered metals | Do not polish anything unless the Playbook documents it. Many households want the patina and removing it is not reversible.
Painted and lacquered surfaces | Barely damp, no abrasive, no solvent. Matte and chalk paint mark permanently under any scrubbing at all.
Leather | Dry dust and vacuum with a soft brush. No water, no household cleaner, no product at all unless documented. Conditioning is scheduled work, not weekly work.
Upholstery | Vacuum with the upholstery tool, cushions rotated and plumped. Blot spills immediately with plain water. Never apply a cleaning product to an unknown fabric.
Glass and mirrors | Product onto the cloth, never sprayed onto the glass, because runoff destroys mirror silvering and window seals from the edge inward.

Screens and displays | Dry microfiber, or a screen-specific product on the cloth. Never household glass cleaner, never alcohol, never anything ammonia-based, all of which strip the anti-glare coating permanently.
Acid on stone: vinegar, citrus, lime scale remover, most bathroom cleaners.
Water on wood, laminate or cork beyond barely damp.
Steam on any wood, laminate, or unsealed surface.
Abrasives on quartz, nonstick, acrylic, matte paint, or brushed metal.
Bleach on stainless steel, wool, stone, or grout.
Beater bar on wool, silk, loop pile or antique rugs.
Alcohol or glass cleaner on screens.
Any two products mixed. Bleach with ammonia produces chlorine gas, and both are in ordinary household cleaners.

If you have already used the wrong thing, stop, rinse with plain water where that is safe, dry, and tell the client the same day. Damage caught in the first hour is sometimes recoverable. Damage discovered next week never is, and concealing it is a far more serious matter than causing it.
Any surface where you were unsure and used plain water instead, so the household can tell you what it is.
Sealant failure: water no longer beading on stone, grout darkening, wood finish gone dull or patchy in a traffic path.
Wear that a household will not notice until it is expensive: a traffic lane in a carpet, a rug fringe fraying, a floorboard cupping, a counter edge chipping.
Anything you did that you would want them to know about, including a product you tried and a mark you could not remove.
Anything needing a specialist rather than us, particularly silk and antique rugs, leather conditioning, and stone resealing.
The target is ready, not perfect. A living room that has been styled rather than reset reads as somebody else’s room, and a family will feel it before they can name it.
Cushions plumped and returned to the household’s own arrangement, not squared into a hotel line.
Throws folded or draped the way this family drapes them. Photograph it on an early visit if it is particular.
Remote controls in their documented place, together, batteries checked. This is small and it is one of the things households mention.
Charging cables coiled and left where they live rather than tidied out of sight.
Books and magazines straightened, never reordered and never put away.
Furniture returned to its footprint. Check against the marks in the carpet rather than by eye.
Read, then look from the doorway. What changed since last week tells you what this room is actually being used for.
Clear and collect. Dishes and glasses to the kitchen, laundry to the hamper, anything belonging to another room into a single carry.
Dust top to bottom. Light fittings and fan blades, frames, shelves, sills, skirting, and the tops of everything tall.
Surfaces and glass, per WK-STD-007.
Upholstery. Vacuum with the brush tool, into the crevices, cushions lifted and rotated on the documented cadence.
Reset. Cushions, throws, remotes, furniture position.
Floor last, then check from the doorway the way the family will see it.
Screens are dry microfiber or a screen-specific product on the cloth. Never household glass cleaner, never alcohol.
Never unplug anything to clean around it, and never move a device that is on or charging.
Do not change a setting, an input, or a volume, and do not turn anything off that you found on.
Cables dusted and tidied only into the household’s existing management. Do not re-route or re-bundle.
Speaker grilles and vents are brushed dry, never sprayed.
Toys returned to the household’s existing system, not to a better one.
Small parts, batteries and anything a younger child could reach are a same-day flag rather than a report line.
Never discard artwork, schoolwork, or anything a child made.
If the room is being defeated by toy volume week after week, name it plainly in the report and propose a reset. Do not solve it quietly on a Tuesday.
Hearths swept per the documented cadence. Never handle ash you are not certain is cold, and never vacuum ash with a household vacuum.
Note glass doors, screens and anything that suggests a chimney sweep is due.
Plants per WK-STD-009. Over-watering is the usual error.
Seasonal decoration is put up and taken down as scheduled work, not as a weekly improvisation.
Window coverings dusted, checked for cord safety in homes with young children, and adjusted to the household’s documented daily position.
The table is the point of the room. Clear, cleaned to its material, and reset to how the household keeps it.
Table leaves, protective pads and linens noted and cared for on their own cadence.
Chairs checked for looseness, which is both wear and a safety matter.
Where a dining table has become a working or storage surface, that is a systems observation worth naming rather than clearing away each week.
Restyle, rearrange, or improve the layout.
Reorder books, put away reading, or close anything left open on purpose.
Discard anything, including what looks like packaging or scrap paper.
Adjust devices, settings, or anything mid-use.
Use scent or spray unless the household documents it.
Wear on upholstery, rugs and traffic paths.
Anything loose, wobbling, or coming apart.
Batteries, bulbs and consumables replaced or needed.
Systems observations: what this room is losing the fight against, named without judgment.
A photograph of the done state from the doorway.
Tier 2 floor under WK-STD-000 Section 1. This room is where the confidentiality promise is most directly tested, and the provisions in Sections 2 and 3 are not overridden by preference.

You never read. Not a letter, not a bill, not a statement, not a sticky note, not a document face up on a desk. If a task would require you to read something to decide what to do with it, that task is not in scope.
Paper is squared into a stack in the place it already occupies. It is not sorted, not moved to another surface, and not put into a drawer.
Where the Playbook documents categories and a destination, you may route by an external marker only: an unopened envelope, a delivery slip, a labeled tray. Never by content.
Never open sealed mail. Never unfold something folded.
Never photograph a desk, a document, a screen, or a whiteboard, in any report, ever.
Never shred anything. Shredding is irreversible and the decision belongs to the household alone, however obviously disposable something appears.
Confidential waste never goes into a general bin. Where a household has a documented secure disposal, use it. Where it does not, leave the item and flag it.
If you find something distressing or sensitive, put it back exactly as it was, say nothing, and carry on. That is the entire procedure.
Never wake, unlock, touch or move a device.
Never unplug anything, including to clean behind it. Work around cables rather than through them.
Never close a laptop, dismiss a notification, or answer a ringing phone.
Screens are cleaned dry with microfiber, or with a screen-specific product applied to the cloth, and only where the device is off and the Playbook permits it.
Keyboards are brushed or air-dusted, never wiped wet and never rearranged.
If a screen is visible and displaying something, clean elsewhere in the room and come back. Do not read it and do not mention it.
Dust top to bottom around equipment rather than moving it. Photograph a complicated desk before touching anything near it.
Vacuum floors and under the desk where cables allow safe access. Never pull a cable to reach further.
Empty the general waste bin. Check first that nothing in it is confidential, and if you are unsure, leave it and flag it.
Wipe surfaces to the material standard in WK-STD-007, working around anything you were not asked to move.
Restock printer paper and documented consumables. Note toner and supplies running low.
Note power strips that are overloaded, cables that are damaged, and anything creating a heat or trip risk.
Room clean, surfaces dusted, floor done.
Every piece of paper in the same place and the same order as you found it.
Every device in the same state you found it: on stays on, open stays open, nothing moved.
Nothing filed, nothing discarded, nothing shredded.
Nothing you saw retained, repeated, or recorded.
Room cleaned, and anything not done because access was blocked or a device was in use.
Safety findings: overloaded power, damaged cable, heat, trip hazard.
Anything you left rather than binned because you could not tell whether it was confidential.
Never a description of any document, screen, or piece of paper, including in general terms.
Tier 1 floor under WK-STD-000 Section 1 for the safety provisions in Sections 2 and 4. Everything else follows the household Playbook, and where the Playbook is silent, this standard.

Never make a decision about a pet’s food, care, medication or wellbeing that is not documented. Not a treat, not a portion change, not a walk route, not a dose. If it is not in the Playbook, contact the client.

section_title: Safety, for the animal and for you
text: Know the household’s door protocol before you open any door, on your first visit and every visit after.

section_title: Safety, for the animal and for you
text: Confirm where the animal is before opening an exterior door, bringing in a delivery, or letting anyone else in.

section_title: Safety, for the animal and for you
text: Check gates and fencing where the pet has outdoor access, and flag anything loose the same day.

section_title: Safety, for the animal and for you
text: If an animal gets out, call the client immediately. Do not spend twenty minutes searching first.

section_title: Safety, for the animal and for you
text: Dogs | Xylitol, found in sugar-free gum, mints, some peanut butters and baked goods, is the most dangerous and least known. Also chocolate, grapes and raisins, onions and garlic, macadamia nuts, alcohol, and raw yeast dough.

section_title: Safety, for the animal and for you
text: Cats | Lilies of any kind are fatal to cats, including pollen brushed onto fur, and a bouquet delivered to the house is the usual route in. Also onions and garlic, and many essential oils.

section_title: Safety, for the animal and for you
text: Birds | Fumes from overheated nonstick cookware are fatal to birds within minutes, as are many aerosols, scented candles and strong cleaning products. Ventilation is not optional in a household with birds.

section_title: Safety, for the animal and for you
text: All pets | Cleaning products left accessible or on a wet floor an animal will walk across and then lick. Medication dropped on a floor. Antifreeze. String, ribbon and hair ties.

section_title: Safety, for the animal and for you
text: If flowers arrive at a house with a cat, check for lilies before they are put in water and flag it to the client immediately rather than arranging them.

section_title: Safety, for the animal and for you
text: Never leave a cleaning product, a bucket, or a freshly treated wet floor accessible to an animal.

section_title: Safety, for the animal and for you
text: If you believe a pet has eaten something it should not have, contact the client immediately and do not wait to see whether it passes.

section_title: Safety, for the animal and for you
text: You are never required to work with an animal that frightens you or behaves aggressively. Secure yourself, leave the area, and contact your Well Kept contact. This will never count against you.

section_title: Safety, for the animal and for you
text: Do not attempt to handle, restrain, medicate or discipline an animal that is not documented as yours to handle.

section_title: Safety, for the animal and for you
text: Report any bite, scratch or near miss the same day, however minor, and however embarrassing.
Feeding. Documented food, documented portion, documented time. Measured, not estimated. Fresh water at every visit, bowl washed rather than topped up.
Walking. Documented route, duration and equipment. Never off-leash unless documented. Never a new route without asking.
Cleanup. Litter trays, crates, bedding and accident cleanup per the Playbook, using pet-safe products only. Wash hands thoroughly afterward and before any food task.
Medication. Only where the Playbook documents that you administer it, and only exactly as written. Never adjust a dose or a time. Note every dose given.
Grooming. Only what is documented. Never trim nails, cut fur, or bathe an animal without explicit instruction.
Eating or drinking noticeably more or less. Water intake changes are worth reporting on their own.
Limping, stiffness, reluctance on stairs, or a change in how the animal moves.
Changes in the litter tray or in toileting.
Lethargy, hiding, or a change in temperament.
Anything on the skin or coat you had not seen before.
Over-watering kills far more houseplants than neglect does. Follow the documented schedule, not instinct, and when the Playbook and your judgment disagree, follow the Playbook and note it.
Water on the documented schedule and in the documented amount. Where a household documents checking the soil first, do that rather than watering by calendar.
Never let a pot stand in collected water. Empty saucers and cachepots after watering, which is where root rot begins.
Never move a plant to a better spot. Light, draft and radiator position are usually deliberate, and a plant that has acclimatized to a position suffers when moved.
Never repot, prune, fertilize or treat a plant unless it is documented.
Dust leaves gently where documented, supported from underneath, with plain water and never a leaf shine product.
Rotate for even growth only where the household documents it.
Watering needs fall substantially in winter, and the most common seasonal error is continuing a summer schedule into December.
Note plants sitting against a cold window or above a radiator when the heating comes on.
Flag anything outgrowing its pot, in autumn, so repotting can be scheduled rather than improvised.
Give a pet anything to eat or drink that is not documented, including a small treat.
Change a portion, a schedule, a route, or a dose.
Let an animal outside unsupervised where that is not documented.
Administer medication you have not been documented and instructed to give.
Take a pet to a vet, or make any care decision, without reaching the client, except where the Playbook documents an emergency authorization.
Bring an animal a toy, a treat, or anything from outside the household.
Photograph a pet for anything other than the household’s own record, and never for any Well Kept use.
Move, repot, prune, or feed a plant outside the documented instruction.
Care delivered: feeding, walking, cleanup, doses given and at what time.
Observations about the animal, described and not diagnosed.
Supplies low: food, litter, medication approaching the end of a course.
Safety findings: gates, fencing, anything accessible that should not be.
Plant condition and anything needing attention or a season ahead of it.
Anything delivered to the house that is a hazard, including flowers in a household with a cat.
Tier 1 floor under WK-STD-000 Section 1 for Sections 3 and 5. Everything else follows the household Playbook, and where it is silent, this standard.
