Products the household keeps and wants used, by surface.
Products the household refuses, and why where they have said. Sensitivities, allergies, pets, scent, environmental preference.
Anything that may never be bleached, scrubbed, or laundered.
Where products are stored, and where they must be kept out of reach.
Who buys them and against what spend limit.

section_title: When the record has a gap
text: Use the mildest thing that could work. Plain water and a microfiber cloth handles more than people expect and damages nothing.

section_title: When the record has a gap
text: Note the gap in the report so the Playbook can be completed. A gap logged once is a gap closed forever.

section_title: When the record has a gap
text: Never improvise on natural stone, wood, screens, leather, or anything you cannot identify. Leave it and ask.

section_title: When the record has a gap
text: Where a household keeps no product suitable for a surface they want cleaned, propose one rather than working around it indefinitely.

Never mix two products. Not in a bucket, not on a surface, not one after another without rinsing in between. Bleach with ammonia produces chloramine gas. Bleach with any acid, including vinegar and many toilet and lime scale cleaners, produces chlorine gas. Both are in ordinary cupboards and both send people to hospital every year.
Ventilate before you start, not after you notice the smell.
Gloves for anything beyond a general-purpose spray. Eye protection for anything caustic, including oven and drain products.
Products stay in their original containers with their original labels. If you cannot read a label, you do not use the product.

Never decant any cleaning product into a food or drink container. A bleach solution in a water bottle is one of the most common serious household poisonings, and it happens in homes where everybody knew better.
Never mix a working solution stronger than the label states. Stronger does not clean better and it damages surfaces and skin.
If you feel unwell, dizzy, or your eyes or throat sting, leave the room, get air, and report it the same day.
Never above a food surface or a food-preparation area, and never above where dishes are stored.
In any household with a child under five or a pet, everything hazardous is stored per the documented arrangement, and finding something within reach is a same-day flag rather than a report line.
Bleach stored away from acids and ammonia products, not beside them.
Nothing stored near heat, and nothing flammable stored near a boiler, furnace or water heater.
Return everything to its documented place at the end of the visit. Nothing is left out, on a counter, or in a bathroom.
Bleach degrades within about six months even sealed. An old bottle is close to salt water and a household using it believes it is disinfecting when it is not.
General cleaning products hold roughly six months to two years. Check dates and note anything past.
Stored batteries, including smoke and carbon monoxide detector batteries, are replaced at least annually.
Opened paint holds six months to five years.
Fire extinguishers are inspected annually and replaced against the specific unit’s interval.
These belong in the household’s replacement registry rather than in your memory. Note dates as you find them.

Nothing that has been used in one household is used in another before it has been laundered. Cloths, mop heads and reusable pads travel between homes only clean. This is the same principle as separating cloths within a house, applied at the scale that actually matters.
Cloths are separated by zone and never cross: kitchen, bathroom surfaces, toilet, glass, floors. A cloth that has touched a toilet touches nothing else at all.
Where the household provides color-coded cloths, follow their scheme and record it. Where they do not, carry your own coded set.
Every cloth used leaves with you and goes to the laundry. Nothing is rinsed and rehung for the following week.
Mop heads are laundered between households, never between rooms in the same household unless one is a bathroom.
Buckets emptied, rinsed and dried after every use, and never used for two different solutions.
Vacuums: check and empty before you start rather than after. A full bag or canister cleans badly and a blocked filter overheats the motor.
Never carry vacuum debris from one household into another. Empty and check between homes.
Check the brush roll for wound hair and thread every visit. This is what kills a vacuum and it is a two-minute fix.
Confirm the beater bar setting before touching any rug, per WK-STD-007.
Report any equipment fault the same day. Working around broken equipment costs more than replacing it.
General-purpose neutral cleaner, glass cleaner, bathroom cleaner, a degreaser, and a wood-safe cleaner.
Microfiber cloths in the five coded zones, enough for every room in the house without reuse.
Non-scratch pads, a soft brush, and a toilet brush where the household does not provide one.
Gloves, bin liners, a marker and tape for labeling, and a spare mesh laundry bag.
Restock at the end of the visit, never the start. A kit checked when you finish means the next visit begins complete rather than beginning with an inventory.
Household-specific products stay in the household and never travel in the kit.
Supplies low or out, with enough notice to buy calmly.
Gaps in the documented product set, and any surface you cleaned with water because you were unsure.
Anything stored unsafely, particularly within reach of a child or a pet.
Any product you used that was not previously documented, and why.
Tier 1 floor under WK-STD-000 Section 1 for Section 2. Everything else follows the household Playbook, and where it is silent, this standard.
Weekly, if documented: the walked path kept clear, the sentinel checks in Section 3, and anything the household has specifically scoped.
Not weekly: sorting, decluttering, organizing, or moving stored belongings. That is reset work, scoped and priced separately.
Never in scope: anything requiring a ladder, anything involving tools or equipment, and anything in Section 2.
You do not climb, you do not lift alone, and you do not touch anything you cannot identify. There is nothing in a garage or an attic worth an injury or an exposure.
No ladders and no pull-down attic stairs. Falls are the most common serious injury in this work and attic stairs are the most common cause. If something requires height, it is a vendor task.
Never disturb unknown dust, insulation or damaged material in an older home. Homes built before the late 1970s may contain asbestos and lead. Note it, leave it, and never sand, scrape or sweep it.
Never dry-sweep or vacuum rodent droppings. Dry disturbance aerosolizes what makes them dangerous. Do not touch them. Report them and let a professional handle it.
Never handle unlabeled chemicals, old paint, solvents, fuel, propane or pool chemicals. Do not move them, consolidate them, or dispose of them.
Never touch an electrical panel beyond noting its condition, and never anything with exposed or damaged wiring.
Do not work in a space with poor lighting, poor ventilation, or standing water. Report it instead.
Do not lift anything heavy or awkward alone, and never above shoulder height.
If a space smells of gas, fuel, or anything sharp and chemical, leave, ventilate if you safely can, and call the client immediately.

Water heater | Look for rust at the base, damp on the floor around it, or staining on the pan. A water heater usually weeps for weeks before it fails. Note its age from the nameplate once, into the appliance registry.
Furnace and HVAC | Filter condition and date, unusual noise, damp around the unit, and a condensate line that is dripping or blocked.

Sump pump | Confirm present, confirm the battery backup is present or confirmed absent, and note standing water in the pit. The same storm that floods a basement often takes the power out, so a pump without its own backup fails exactly when it is needed.
Washer supply hoses | Where laundry is in these spaces, per WK-STD-006. Bulging, cracking, corrosion at the coupling.
Floor, walls and foundation | New cracks, efflorescence, a damp line on a wall, or a musty smell that was not there. Photograph anything you can, so change over time is visible.
Ceiling below a bathroom | The first sign of an upstairs leak nearly always appears on a basement or garage ceiling. Look up.
Detectors | Smoke and carbon monoxide, present and functioning, particularly near a furnace or an attached garage.
Pests | Droppings, gnawed packaging, nesting material, insect activity. Report and do not disturb.

section_title: Routine work where it is scoped
text: Keep the walked path and the route to any shutoff, panel or exit completely clear. This is a safety requirement, not tidiness.

section_title: Routine work where it is scoped
text: Sweep or vacuum hard floors where documented, wet conditions permitting.

section_title: Routine work where it is scoped
text: Wipe surfaces and shelving only where documented, and never move stored belongings to do it.

section_title: Routine work where it is scoped
text: Manage recycling and waste staging where that lives here.

section_title: Routine work where it is scoped
text: Note seasonal items that will be needed soon and are buried, early enough to be useful.
Move, consolidate, or dispose of any chemical, paint, fuel or unknown container.
Discard anything at all. What looks like junk in a garage is very often not.
Open, unpack, or look inside stored boxes and containers.
Reorganize storage, however much better it could be. Note it and propose a reset.
Touch tools, equipment, or anything with a blade or a motor.
Work in the space if you are alone in the house and the conditions concern you.
Everything from the sentinel sweep, described and not diagnosed, with photographs where possible.
Anything blocking a path, a shutoff, a panel or an exit.
Safety findings you did not touch: chemicals, wiring, damaged material, pests.
Filters and consumables due.

Ages against expected life, captured once into the replacement registry: a water heater at eight to twelve years, an HVAC system at fifteen to twenty, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors at ten, a roof by its material’s rated life. An appliance approaching its window is a planning conversation, not an emergency.
Seasonal items that should surface soon.
Anything suggesting a reset would earn its cost.

Ours: the entry approach and steps, porch and stoop, the immediate transition zone, package and delivery areas, waste and recycling staging, outdoor furniture and cushions, the grill and outdoor kitchen where documented, and anything a family walks across to get inside.
Vendor work, which we coordinate rather than do: lawn, planting beds, tree work, gutters, roof, pressure washing, snow clearance beyond the immediate path, pool, and anything structural.
Never ours: anything requiring a ladder, a power tool, a chemical treatment, or work at height.
You do not go up a ladder, onto a roof, or onto anything you have to climb. You do not use power equipment. If a task needs either, it is a vendor task and noting it is the whole of your job.

Ice and snow on steps and paths is a same-day matter. Where clearance is documented as ours, do the walked path and treat it. Where it is not, flag it to the client immediately rather than waiting for the report.
Moss and algae on shaded steps and paving are as slippery as ice and are usually ignored until somebody falls. Report them.
Check handrails, step edges and decking boards for movement every visit. A loose handrail is a same-day flag.
Note exterior lighting that has failed, which is a security matter as much as a safety one.
Do not work outside in lightning, high wind, or extreme heat or cold. Reschedule the outdoor portion and say so.
Sweep the approach, steps, porch and immediate paths. Clear leaves from steps and from any drain or grate you can reach safely.
Wipe the front door, handle, bell and any glass. This is the first thing every visitor touches and it is almost always overlooked.
Cobwebs cleared from the entry, lights and door frame.
Doormats shaken, both sides, and the surface underneath cleaned.
Outdoor furniture wiped, cushions checked for damp and stored per the documented arrangement.
Waste and recycling containers taken out and returned per the collection schedule, and rinsed on the documented cadence.
Grill cleaned and covered where documented. Note gas level so a family is not discovering it on a Saturday.

Late summer into fall | Gutters cleared before leaf fall, booked not done. Heating serviced before it is needed. Children’s outerwear and boots sized before the first cold week. Hose bibs drained and hoses disconnected before the first freeze, which is the single most common and most expensive seasonal miss. Salt and ice melt bought before the first forecast.
Winter | Paths and steps kept safe. Salt damage to floors and paving watched. Outdoor furniture stored or covered. Check that anything vulnerable to freezing is not sitting in an unheated garage.

Late winter into spring | Winter damage noted while it is still worth reporting. Furniture and cushions back out and cleaned. Grill checked and gas replaced. Screens and windows. Air conditioning serviced before the first warm week.
Summer | Outdoor living kept usable. Watering per the documented schedule. Sun damage and fading noted on furniture and fabrics. Insect activity around doors and eaves reported.
Anything needing a vendor, named early enough to book rather than emergency.
Safety findings: ice, moss, loose rails, failed lighting, uneven paving.
Seasonal items coming due, a season ahead.
Wear and weather damage: paint, decking, furniture, fabrics.
Pest activity around the exterior.
Tier 2 floor under WK-STD-000 Section 1. Observance is recorded in Playbook Sections 12, 13 and 16 as caution-flagged fields, and it is followed exactly.
The failure here is almost never disrespect. It is a House Manager being helpful in a way nobody asked for, on a day when the household needed something specific done in a specific way.

Separation of meat and dairy where kept: separate dishes, utensils, boards, sinks, cloths, storage and sometimes appliances. Know which is which before you touch anything, and if you are not certain, stop and ask.
Never move an item between the two systems, and never wash them together.
Follow the documented sourcing rules for anything bought or put away.
If you make a mistake, say so immediately. A household can correct a kashering error it knows about. It cannot correct one it does not.

Rest-day observances reshape the service window. In a Shabbat household, the pre-sundown preparation on Friday is itself the service, and the window closes hard. Work to the documented timing rather than the usual schedule.
Daily prayer times are quiet windows. Where they are documented, work elsewhere in the home and do not use noisy equipment. Do not enter the room being used.

Fasting periods invert the rhythm of the kitchen. In a Ramadan household, suhoor before dawn and iftar after sunset reshape the whole week, including grocery timing, meal preparation and delivery windows.
Be aware of what a fasting household needs from you and be discreet about your own eating and drinking in the home during a fast.
Eid, Diwali, Lunar New Year, Passover, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur all move. Confirm dates each year against the household’s own record rather than a general calendar.

Preparation traditions matter as much as the day. A pre-Passover deep clean has a specific scope and a hard deadline. A Lunar New Year household cleans before the new year and specifically not during its first days, and cleaning on the wrong day is worse than not cleaning at all.
Anticipate these the way you anticipate anything else. They belong in the calendar weeks ahead, not the week of.

Sacred texts, objects and images may have placement and orientation rules: a text kept on the highest shelf, an object never placed on the floor, an image never turned to face a particular way. Follow them exactly and never relocate any of them.
Some items are never touched at all, by anyone outside the household. Where that is documented, clean around them and do not dust them.
A prayer rug or mat may never be stepped on or vacuumed over. Know where they are.
Shoes-off households set your own practice at the door, per WK-STD-003. Carry dedicated indoor shoes or covers.
Where a room is documented as private, off-limits, or requiring permission to enter, that is a confirmed fact and not an oversight.
Cookware may carry its own rules, including a seasoned wok or heirloom cast iron on the do-not-soap list, per WK-STD-001.
Flower and gift customs vary sharply. White flowers read as funerary in several cultures. Clocks, certain numbers, and some colors carry meanings that turn a kindness into an insult.
Never improvise a gesture in a household whose observance you do not know well. Check the Playbook, and where it is silent, ask before rather than apologize after.
Food gestures are governed entirely by dietary law and by WK-STD-002. A treat that breaches kashrut or halal is not a small error.
Seasonal decoration is never assumed. Do not put anything up that the household has not documented.
Follow documented norms about greeting, physical contact, modesty of dress, and being alone in the home with a member of the household.
Do not ask questions out of curiosity. Ask only what you need in order to do the work correctly.
Never comment on, compare, or explain a household’s practice, to them or to anyone else.
If your own observance requires an accommodation, raise it with Well Kept rather than the client. It will be handled as scheduling, not as an issue.
Gaps in the observance record you had to ask about, so the Playbook closes them.
Upcoming observances and their preparation needs, weeks ahead.
Anything you were unsure about and worked around.
Never a description, explanation, or observation about the household’s practice itself. Record the operational fact and nothing more.
Agree a par level for every consumable the household cares about: paper goods, cleaning supplies, laundry products, batteries, bulbs, pet supplies, and the specific staples in Playbook Section 12.
Check against par every visit and note anything at or below it, rather than waiting for something to run out.
Note what runs out fastest and adjust the par upward. Note what never moves and adjust it down, since storage is finite and a household is paying for both.
Order or add to the list per the documented method and the documented spend limit.
Folded to the standard in WK-STD-000, folded edges facing out, stacked by type and by bed or bath size.
Sheet sets stored inside one of their own pillowcases so a set is never reassembled from a shelf.
Rotate from the bottom, so wear spreads evenly rather than falling on the top two sets forever.
Keep guest linen separate from household linen and clearly distinguished.
Out-of-season bedding stored clean, never soiled, and never in a space where it will take on a smell.
Inventory once a season against what the household actually needs. Note thin, pilled, mismatched, or elastic that has gone.
Do not reorganize an existing system. Maintain it and propose changes.
Bed made with fresh linen, changed on a documented cadence whether or not it has been used. Linen that has sat for two months is not fresh however clean it is.
Surfaces dusted, floor done, and the room aired on the documented cadence.
Empty closet space and hangers available, and a clear surface for a suitcase.
Nothing of the household’s stored in the room where a guest will need the space.
Working lamp and reachable outlet on each side of the bed. Check the bulbs.
Window coverings functioning and able to darken the room.
Fresh towels, hand towel and washcloth, hung to the standard.
Paper stocked with a spare visible.
Soap and documented toiletries present and not nearly empty.
Cleaned every visit regardless of use, and nothing personal to the household left out.
Confirm dates, numbers and any documented needs early. Allergies, dietary requirements and mobility all belong in the Playbook before the guest arrives, not after.
Fresh linen and towels regardless of when they were last changed.
Check the room a guest will actually use as a guest would: sit on the bed, look for where a phone charges, notice what is missing.
Note anything the household will want to buy in time to buy it calmly.
Strip and launder everything, including anything unused that was out during the stay.
Return the room to guest-ready rather than leaving it until it is needed again.
Check for anything left behind and set it aside in the documented place, unopened and unexamined.
Anything at or below par.
Linen needing replacement, with enough notice to buy without urgency.
Guest-ready status, and anything that would be missing if someone arrived tomorrow.
Items left behind by a guest.
Par levels that need adjusting up or down.

section_title: The signature ritual and the traditions registry
text: Every household has one repeatable, named touch that is never skipped, on any visit, however hard. It is recorded in the Playbook and it is identity rather than a nice-to-have. When the clock runs out, you must already know which touch is which, and this is the one that survives.

section_title: The signature ritual and the traditions registry
text: Traditions are kept, never improved. A tradition altered is a tradition broken, even when the alteration is better.

section_title: The signature ritual and the traditions registry
text: A once-only moment a family would grieve missing is held in the memory and milestone register, and quietly marked: the outfit ready, the photo tradition kept.

section_title: The signature ritual and the traditions registry
text: These belong to the delight layer and are never billed, never proposed as an upgrade, and never used as evidence of value in a scope conversation.
A primary timeline, and a contingency at every key risk point. Each decided during planning rather than under pressure. The value of a contingency is entirely in having chosen it while calm.
Vendor reconfirmation at 24 to 48 hours out, as routine practice. Not as a response to a problem. A confirmation call made because something felt wrong is already late.
Day-of contacts, not the account manager who sold the package. The person who will actually be in the van on Saturday, with a number that reaches them on Saturday.
Allergens and dietary requirements confirmed for every attendee where the household has them, per WK-STD-002.
Access, parking and delivery windows planned in advance, and anyone entering the home documented ahead of time per WK-STD-020.
A written order of the day that a covering House Manager could run from cold.
Rental returns processed against their deadlines, with the deadlines logged rather than remembered.
Final vendor payment reconciled and recorded.
Thank-you notes tracked: who, for what, sent or outstanding.
A lost-and-found sweep, with anything found set aside unopened and unexamined.
A short debrief note that feeds the next event. What ran well, what ran late, which vendor to use again and which not. Without it, the household relearns the same lesson every year.

The recurring-guests registry records who stays, their room setup and their preferences. A returning guest should find the room the way they left it last time, which is one of the cheapest and most memorable things a household can offer.
Confirm dates, numbers, allergies, dietary needs and mobility requirements before arrival rather than after.
Follow the guest-and-visitor policy about whether anyone may be present while you work. This is a privacy and liability boundary, not a preference.
The reversible childproofing kit is staged before arrival: outlet covers, the gate, the toy drawer, the booster seat.
Allergy-checked against Playbook Section 1 for the visiting child, not only the household.
Everything within a small child’s reach reviewed: medication, cleaning products, cords and blind pulls, anything that tips, small objects, the pool or water access.
Food handling shifts to the children’s provisions in WK-STD-002 Section 7 for the duration, including the cutting rules for under-fours.
Fully removed after. The home is safe on Saturday and a gallery again on Monday, and the reversal is as much a part of the job as the setup.
Staged and reversible, documented in advance rather than improvised in week one.
What changes: visit timing, what the remaining adult can no longer absorb, meal patterns, which tasks move from shared to covered, and the tasks the absent person normally owned.
Restored on return rather than left running, and the return is planned as deliberately as the departure.
For a rotating-shift household, the quiet-time window is a fact that is periodically reconfirmed, never one set at intake and left to go stale.
Absence is sensitive information. Occupancy patterns are Restricted data under WK-SOP-019 and are never discussed outside service delivery.

Logistics only. Day, time, who drives, what preparation the home needs before or after. Never the reason and never the content. This is the same privacy boundary Section 1 gives to medication, and it applies just as strictly to a therapy appointment, a recovery meeting, or a place of worship.
The cultural check comes first, always, per WK-STD-014 Section 5. Flower and gift customs vary sharply and a kindness that lands wrong is worse than none.
Allergens and dietary law govern every food gesture, per WK-STD-002.
Sympathy sendings follow the bereavement rules in WK-STD-016 Section 2 for warmth and timing, and nothing is ever proposed alongside them.
A gesture is never branded and a moment is never a marketing asset. A branded gesture is marketing and an unbranded one is care.
Where a household runs an outer-circle gift program, work from the person registry, its dates, gift history and sensitivity flags, rather than from memory.
Improvise a tradition, alter one, or skip the signature ritual.
Improvise precedence, seating or ceremonial order.
Leave childproofing in place after a visit, or remove it before one is over.
Record or repeat the reason behind any standing commitment.
Discuss a household’s absence pattern with anyone.
Propose an add-on in proximity to a loss, per WK-STD-016.
Confirm a vendor only once, or rely on the number of the person who sold the package.
Events upcoming, with their run-of-show status and anything still unconfirmed.
Post-event items outstanding: returns, payments, thank-you notes, and the debrief note itself.
Guest arrivals coming, and anything the household will want to buy in time.
Childproofing staged or removed, and any hazard found during the review.
Mode changes: solo coverage entered or ended, quiet-time windows reconfirmed.
Traditions kept, recorded plainly so a covering House Manager sees they are real.

Tier 2 floor under WK-STD-000 Section 1 for Section 2. Device, account and platform security are governed by WK-SOP-019 and are not repeated here. This document covers spending a household’s money, which SOP-019 does not.

section_title: Account access, and the rule that governs it
text: You never hold a client’s password. Not written down, not in your own password manager, not typed into your own device, not memorized and reused. WK-SOP-019 states that shared logins do not exist in any role for any reason, and a client’s retail account is a shared login by nature. The workaround is not more careful password handling. It is not using a password at all.

section_title: Account access, and the rule that governs it
text: Delegated access | Preferred. Most major retailers support a household, family or authorized-user arrangement that issues you your own login under the client’s account. You get your own credentials, the client keeps visibility and can revoke instantly, and no password changes hands.

section_title: Account access, and the rule that governs it
text: A Well Kept account, reimbursed | For generic supplies with no household-specific account needed. Purchased on the company account and billed through, per the documented arrangement.

section_title: Account access, and the rule that governs it
text: A household device with a saved session | Acceptable where the device never leaves the home and the session was set up by the client. You use it in the house. You do not move it, and you do not extend the session to any other device.

section_title: Account access, and the rule that governs it
text: The client places the order | Always available and never a failure. You build the cart, send it, and manage everything after: tracking, receiving, putting away, returns.

section_title: Account access, and the rule that governs it
text: If a client offers you their password, decline warmly and propose delegated access instead. "I am not allowed to hold it, and there is a better way that keeps you in control" is the whole conversation.

section_title: Account access, and the rule that governs it
text: If you already hold one, say so now. Nobody will be in trouble for raising it and it will be replaced with a proper arrangement.

section_title: Account access, and the rule that governs it
text: Never save a card, an address, or a login to a browser or device that is not the household’s own.

section_title: Account access, and the rule that governs it
text: Never use a household’s account to buy anything for another household, for Well Kept, or for yourself. Not even briefly, not even repaid the same day.
Standing | Replenishment against documented par levels | No approval. Same brand, same size, same place. Default cap of $75 per item and $250 per week unless the Playbook sets otherwise.
Ask first | Anything new, anything above the cap, anything not on the list | Client approval before purchase, through the platform so there is a record. Never a verbal yes you cannot evidence.
Never | Durables, appliances, credit, subscriptions, anything recurring | Not on your authority under any circumstance, however clearly the household would want it and however small the amount.
A cap is per household and per week, not per errand. Do not split a purchase across two trips to stay under it.
Never spend your own money and seek reimbursement. If the household route is unavailable, the purchase waits and you say so.
Urgency does not raise your authority. A household needing something today needs a text, not a decision made on their behalf.
Substitute freely: a different size of the same product, the same product from a different store, a documented alternative the Playbook already names.
Ask first: a different brand, a different formulation, anything more expensive, anything the household has not bought before.

Never substitute at all: anything touching an allergy, a dietary law, a medical need, a documented sensitivity, or a specific product a household has said they insist on. WK-STD-002 governs and a substitution there is a safety event, not a shopping decision.
When you are unsure, buy nothing and ask. An unbought item is an inconvenience. A wrong one is waste and a small breach of trust.
You never start, change, pause, upgrade, downgrade or cancel a subscription. Not one. Note it and propose it.

Where a household’s subscriptions or auto-deliveries are misfiring, sending too much, too often, or a tier nobody uses, that is exactly the kind of finding worth naming. It is flagged and proposed, never acted on.

Stored value belongs to the household: gift cards, prepaid accounts, class packages. Track balances and expiry into the registry, use them only where the Playbook documents it, and flag anything approaching expiry early enough to be used.
Never consolidate, transfer or move stored value between accounts.
Every purchase is logged in the platform with what, where, why, and how much. If it is not in the app, it did not happen.
Photograph every receipt, per WK-SOP-019. A digital receipt is captured the same way.
Reconcile against the household’s documented cadence, and report anything you cannot account for the same day.
Never a purchase without a record, even a small one, even one you were told not to worry about.
Combine what can wait into one order rather than placing four. Less packaging at the door, less receiving work, and fewer delivery windows to plan around.
Time orders against the household’s delivery windows and against when somebody is home, per WK-STD-003.
Anything genuinely recurring at a stable interval is a standing-order proposal to the client, never something you set up yourself. Section 5 governs.
Front-load anything with a lead time. An order placed Monday arrives before Friday and one placed Thursday does not.
Track what you ordered through to arrival. An order placed and not followed is worse than one never placed, because the household believes it is handled.
Returns are processed against the documented method, labeled, staged in the outbound zone, and logged with the deadline.
Flag any return window approaching before it closes, not after.
Keep shipping labels, packing slips and boxes until a return window has passed. Do not break down a box for something that may go back.
Wrong, damaged or missing item: photograph it, log it, tell the client the same day, and start the return or replacement only if it falls inside standing authority.
A charge you do not recognize on an account you use: report it to the client and to your Well Kept contact within the hour. Do not investigate it yourself and do not dispute it.
A purchase you made in error: say so immediately. WK-SOP-019 is explicit that concealment rather than error is the firing offense, and that holds here exactly.
Any suspicion an account has been compromised: treat as a security event under WK-SOP-019 and report within the hour.
Everything purchased, with amounts, against which authority.
Anything you did not buy and why, including anything you held for approval.
Substitutions made and substitutions declined.
Returns processed and deadlines approaching.
Subscriptions or auto-deliveries that look wrong, flagged and not acted on.
Stored value approaching expiry.
Anything about account access that is not on one of the four routes in Section 2.
Method is not rushing. Nothing in this document asks you to move faster. It asks you to stop waiting for things you could have started earlier.
Read the Playbook notes, last week’s report, any open flags and their revisit triggers, and the household calendar for the coming fortnight.
Handle what does not need the house: returns processed, supplies ordered, vendors chased, appointments confirmed, errands run.
Cluster errands so a visit is not a series of separate trips. Routing is planned around the household’s neighborhood, not around the order tasks occurred to you.
Carry what the visit needs in one load. A caddy, the supplies, the outbound items from last week. Six trips to the car is fifteen minutes.
1 | Walk the house | Two minutes, every room, touching nothing. What changed since last week is the most useful information you will get, and it shapes everything after.
2 | Perishables and deliveries | Anything on a clock comes first, per WK-STD-002 and WK-STD-003. Nothing else in the house is time-critical.

3 | Start what runs without you | First load of laundry in. Dishwasher on or emptied. Product dwelling in toilets, tubs and anywhere baked on. Anything soaking. These are the only tasks that work while you are elsewhere, so none of them should ever be waiting on you later.
4 | Plan the visit | Thirty seconds. Given what you just saw and how long you have, what is the order and what comes out if time runs short.

Dwell time does the cleaning. Scrubbing is what you do when you did not wait. Almost every product in a bathroom or a kitchen works better after ten minutes than after ten seconds of effort, and those ten minutes are free if you started them before you needed them.
Start where the long-running things live. Kitchen and laundry first, because that is where the machines and the dwell time are.
Work from the furthest point back toward the exit. Upstairs before downstairs, back of the house before the front, so you are never walking across finished floors.
Wet rooms before dry rooms. Kitchen and bathrooms carry the products and the cloths that never touch anything else, so grouping them means one set of cloths and one change of hands rather than four.
Bedrooms and living spaces after, because nothing in them needs to run and they are the rooms most likely to be occupied.
Entryway last, per WK-STD-003. Everything you carry out passes through it.
Return to the machines on their own schedule, not when you happen to finish something. A load sitting wet is time you cannot recover.

section_title: Working a room without going back
text: Bring everything the room needs in one trip. Walking back for a cloth is the most common lost minute in this work.

section_title: Working a room without going back
text: Do each thing once. Clear the whole surface, then clean the whole surface, then reset the whole surface. Not item by item.

section_title: Working a room without going back
text: One circuit around the room in one direction, rather than crossing back and forth.

section_title: Working a room without going back
text: Carry a single collection point for things belonging elsewhere and deliver them on your way out of the room, rather than making a trip per item.

section_title: Working a room without going back
text: Apply the thirty-second rule as you go. Fixing it now is faster than logging it, and WK-STD-000 Section 2 sets the boundaries.

section_title: The week, not just the visit
text: Batch by type across the week rather than by household within a day: all the ordering together, all the vendor calls together, all the appointment confirmations together.

section_title: The week, not just the visit
text: Front-load anything with a lead time. An order placed Monday arrives before Friday. An order placed Thursday does not.

section_title: The week, not just the visit
text: Stage next week while this week is fresh. Five minutes at the end of a visit is worth twenty at the start of the next one.

section_title: The week, not just the visit
text: Group errands geographically and against the households you are seeing that day.

Never cut | Reading the allergen record. Anything in WK-STD-002. The sentinel checks. Anything flagged for revisit. Pets. Medication. Safety findings. The visit report. And the household’s signature ritual, which is never skipped on any visit however hard, because it is identity rather than a nice-to-have.
Protect next | The done state of the kitchen and the primary bathroom, and laundry already started. These are the rooms a household feels first and a load left wet cannot be recovered.
Cut first | Monthly and quarterly cadence work, secondary rooms, anything cosmetic, anything that will keep until next week without consequence.

Say so in the report. What was noticed and deliberately left, with the reason and the intended timing, per WK-STD-000 Section 9. A household is entirely fine with something waiting a week and not fine with discovering it silently did.
If a visit runs short repeatedly, that is a scope conversation rather than a speed problem. Raise it rather than absorbing it week after week.
Never cut a safety item to protect a cosmetic one, and never cut the report to finish a room.
Anything deliberately left, with reason and timing.
Anything that consistently does not fit in the visit, named plainly.
Anything about the house that is costing time and could be solved: a system that fights the household, a supply kept in the wrong place, an appliance that has slowed.
Errands and between-visit work completed.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Tier 2 floor under WK-STD-000 Section 1 for the access provisions in Section 4. Everything else follows the household Playbook, and where it is silent, this standard.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: No markup, ever. The client pays the specialist directly. Well Kept charges a coordination fee and nothing else, and this is stated plainly to the client rather than buried.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Level | Fee | What it covers

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Referral | $75 | A vetted introduction with a brief drawn from the Playbook, so the specialist arrives already knowing the household.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Managed | $150 | The referral plus scheduling, access, and seeing the work through to completion.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Project management | $45 per hour | Sustained coordination across multiple vendors or a long timeline.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Every brief is drawn from the Playbook rather than written fresh, which is what makes the referral worth its fee.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: A brief carries what the specialist needs and nothing more. It is Confidential data under WK-SOP-019 and it never includes anything they do not need to do the work.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Eldercare routing is available at every tier, not gated to Concierge. A family in crisis never needs a tier upgrade to reach a geriatric care manager. This is a decided policy and it is not a judgment call in the moment.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Served, never sold. Through the quarterly review or on a captured signal, never cold and never in the middle of a visit.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Nothing is proposed in proximity to a loss, per WK-STD-016 Section 2. Funeral and estate-settlement routing is governed by the bereavement rules at every mention, always, without exception.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Anticipatory services are proposed before they are needed, which is their entire point. Researching the local eldercare landscape is valuable in advance and nearly worthless in a crisis.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Confirm at booking, then reconfirm at 24 to 48 hours out as routine practice rather than as a response to a problem.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Get the day-of contact, not the account manager. The person who will be in the van.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Brief them on what they need: access, parking, pets, off-limits rooms, surfaces requiring care, and the household’s quiet windows.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Be present for access where documented, and check the work before they leave rather than after.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Photograph vendor work before and after, per WK-SOP-019.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Log everything in the platform: who came, when, what was done, what it cost, what is outstanding.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Cluster where you can. Four vendor visits in a month is four disrupted days for the household. The same four onto one morning is one. Hold non-urgent work until there is something to pair it with, and propose the cluster rather than booking each as it arises.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: A no-show or a late cancellation is reported to the client the same day with a proposed alternative, not simply relayed.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Work below standard is documented with photographs and raised with the client. You do not accept it on their behalf and you do not confront the vendor beyond a factual conversation.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Damage caused by a vendor is photographed and reported immediately, before they leave the property where possible.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Never authorize additional work, approve a change order, or agree a price. That is the client’s, always.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Coordinate through the client rather than directly, unless the Playbook explicitly authorizes direct coordination.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: You do not supervise, direct, correct, or assess anyone the household employs, unless that is documented as your role.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Never criticize their work to the client, never compare, and never take a side in anything between them and the household.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Where work overlaps or conflicts, describe the overlap factually and let the client decide. "The cleaner and I are both doing the bathrooms on Thursday" is useful. A view on who should stop is not.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Never discuss their pay, hours, terms, or performance, and never discuss yours with them.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Where their work creates a safety issue, report it as a safety finding rather than as a complaint.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Never grant access to anyone not documented, without real-time client approval. Not a contractor who says they are expected, not a delivery driver who wants to come in, not a family member you have not met, not a neighbor with a key. This holds however plausible the person is and however inconvenient the refusal.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Anyone expected is documented in advance: name, company, purpose, window.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Verify identity on arrival against what was documented.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Never share an alarm code, a key location, or an entry method with anyone. If a vendor needs access, you provide it in person or the client arranges it.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Never leave a vendor alone in the house unless the household has documented that you may.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Log every entry and exit in the platform.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Occupancy patterns, access methods and codes are Restricted data under WK-SOP-019 and are never discussed with any vendor or partner.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Everyone who entered the home, when, and why.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Vendor work completed, with before and after photographs.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: No-shows, delays, poor work, and damage.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Anything outstanding, with its revisit trigger.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Partner referrals made, at which level, and the fee.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: Any access request you declined, and who made it.

doc_title: Vendors, Partners and Other People in the Home
text: A vendor who is entirely competent but not the right fit, which is a finding worth naming and never acting on unilaterally.
Emergency | Risk to a person, a pet, or the property. Acted on immediately, per WK-SOP-013. Never queued, never triaged further, never left for the report.
Urgent, same day | A deadline today or tomorrow, or something that gets materially worse by waiting. Acknowledged and actioned the same day.
Routine, next visit | The ordinary substance of the service. Acknowledged on receipt, scheduled into the next visit, confirmed done in the report.
Someday, quarterly | Worth doing with no deadline attached. Logged with a revisit trigger and raised at the quarterly review. It does not quietly disappear.
Committed response times run by tier and are recorded in the Playbook. Meet them or say why before they lapse.
Acknowledge everything, immediately, even when you cannot act yet. "I have this and I will handle it Thursday" is a complete response and it is what stops a client wondering.
Never let something sit unclassed. An unclassed request is the one that gets missed.
When you class something lower than the client would have, say so rather than assuming. Most disagreements about responsiveness are disagreements about class.
DO without asking. Act, then report. The household has decided they do not want to be consulted here, and consulting them anyway is a small failure rather than a courtesy.
RECOMMEND and await a yes. Bring it with a recommendation attached rather than as an open question. A recommendation is the work; a list of options is a task handed back.
ASK always. Never act, however obvious. These domains are usually where a household has been burned before, and the boundary matters more than the outcome.
The ladder never overrides a floor. Nothing in the DO column authorizes anything WK-STD-000 Section 1 places above the Playbook.
Situation. Two or three sentences. What is true, without preamble.
Options. Usually two or three, with what each costs and what each trades off.
Recommendation. Yours, stated plainly. Declining to recommend hands the work back.
Needed-by date. The real external deadline, and what happens if it passes.

Early beats complete. Tell them before you have the full picture rather than after. "Something has gone wrong and I am still establishing what" is a better message at nine than a complete account at five.
Lead with the fact. Not the context, not the mitigation, not the apology. The fact, then what you have already done, then what you propose.
No softening that obscures. Warmth is fine. Vagueness is not, and a client who has to ask three questions to find out what happened trusts the fourth answer less.
Own it without collapsing. State what went wrong, take responsibility where it is yours, and move to the fix. Excessive apology makes a client manage your feelings on top of the problem.

Self-report before discovery. A chipped glass, a mark on a wall, a mistake they would almost certainly never have found. Reporting it is the single strongest trust action available in this work. Concealment rather than error is the firing offense, here and throughout the library.
Never refuse flatly and never simply absorb it. Both are failures, and quietly absorbing is the more expensive one because it resets the scope without anyone deciding to.
Say what is in scope, what this would be, and offer the route: an add-on, a partner referral, or a conversation at the review.
Never quote a price or commit Well Kept to anything. Route it.

Log the pattern. The out-of-scope request pattern is the scope conversation in evidence form. Six months of logged requests is a better basis for a tier conversation than anyone’s impression, and it protects the client from being sold something they do not need.
Anything involving safety, a floor conflict, a security event, or a suspected breach goes to your Well Kept contact the same day, and within the hour where WK-SOP-019 requires it.
Anything where a client is unhappy goes up the same day. A concern raised early is a conversation; the same concern found later is a churn risk.
You are never the person who has to win an argument with a client. Raise it and it is handled.
Requests received, how each was classed, and what happened.
Anything awaiting a decision, with its needed-by date.
Out-of-scope requests, logged as pattern rather than as complaint.
Anything you told the client directly rather than waiting for the report, so the record is complete.
Delegation domains that are unset and need setting.
Tier 2 floor under WK-STD-000 Section 1 for Section 2 and Section 3. Everything else follows the household Playbook, and where it is silent, this standard.
A standard done perfectly at the wrong moment is worth very little. December handled in December is a scramble. December handled in October is the product.

section_title: Life events, and when you stop proposing
text: The LIFE-EVENT register (called the bereavement register in earlier drafts; LIFE-EVENT is the canonical name, matching the application status tag in WK-APP-003). In proximity to a death, a suspected job loss, or acute illness or injury, you propose nothing at all. No add-on, no upgrade, no reset, no suggestion, however obviously it would help. You absorb friction quietly instead: meals, guest-ready rooms for visiting family, errands run without being asked. Log the changed rhythms and let the client re-open scope when they are ready.

section_title: Life events, and when you stop proposing
text: Event | What you will see | What you do

section_title: Life events, and when you stop proposing
text: A death in the family | Sudden travel, a quieter house, visiting family, a changed rhythm | Bereavement register. Absorb friction quietly. Propose nothing. Let them re-open scope.

section_title: Life events, and when you stop proposing
text: New job, job loss, or return to office | Commute shifts, home-office use changes, a badge or parking pass, wardrobe turnover | Confirm logistics in the moment. Treat a suspected loss with the bereavement register.

section_title: Life events, and when you stop proposing
text: Separation or divorce | An adult’s belongings thinning, changed sleeping arrangements, tension | Extreme discretion. Never ask. Serve the home as documented until the client raises it.

section_title: Life events, and when you stop proposing
text: Illness or injury | Medical deliveries, mobility aids, a changed appointment rhythm, someone home who was not | Bereavement register while acute. Adjust without being asked. Update flags as they share them.

section_title: Life events, and when you stop proposing
text: An aging parent joins | A room converting, medical equipment arriving, new medication, care visitors | Confirm warmly and practically: new flags, routines, dietary and medical documentation, staff coordination. Have the personal care boundary conversation now, warmly and in advance, per WK-STD-022 Section 2. Waiting for the first request makes it a refusal instead of a fact.

section_title: Life events, and when you stop proposing
text: Child milestones | Learner’s permit paperwork, college mail, a bedroom’s character shifting, new privacy behaviors | Mostly horizon items on schedule. A teen’s room boundary is honored the week it is noticed, never negotiated.

section_title: Life events, and when you stop proposing
text: Move, renovation, major project | Contractor traffic, staging, boxes, photography | Confirm scope impact early: dust, access and zone closures all change the visit.

Seasonal transition, fired before the season and not at it. Late summer for the cold months, late winter for the warm ones. The failure mode is universal: the first cold morning arrives, the coat does not fit, and somebody is scrambling on a school day.

Grade change, which already owns it. The existing cascade carries the outgrown-clothing check alongside the new-teacher gift, the supply list and spirit-day sizing. Fit belongs there rather than in a parallel entry.
Pre-event and pre-trip. The blazer for a chapel day, the swimsuit before a beach trip. Firing a week or two ahead rather than the night before is the entire value of the trigger.

Children’s shoes, quarterly and on their own cadence. Feet outgrow shoes faster than bodies outgrow clothes, the consequence is pain and gait rather than an unflattering hem, and children frequently do not report it. This is the one place a separate trigger earns its keep.

The household line. For children, fit is a maintenance fact and checking it is anticipatory care. For adults it is not. Bodies change for reasons that are private, sometimes medical and sometimes painful, and a House Manager assessing whether an adult’s clothes still fit crosses from service into scrutiny. Adult sizing is owner-initiated only: captured at intake, re-confirmed by asking rather than by looking, and acted on when a household member raises a change.

1. The horizon list | Predictable changes, pre-computed from the roster. A child’s age generates a learner’s permit at fifteen and a driver at sixteen. A school generates its transition years. An aging parent generates a likely arrival. Reviewed each quarter so the next two years are anticipated rather than discovered.

2. The signal protocol | What cannot be predicted must be noticed. You are in the home weekly and you see what changes. Notice, log the same day, confirm at the right moment, adjust. Routine logistics are confirmed gently in the moment. Anything sensitive waits for the right moment or the client.

3. Standing venues | There is always a near-term place to raise something. Every visit through the departure log and its changes-noticed entry. Every quarter at the check-in. Every year at the scope review. Nothing has to wait for a convenient moment to be invented.

4. The household’s own list | A short plain list given to the client of the handful of events worth a text the moment they happen: a move, a new diagnosis, a separation, a death, a new job with a different travel pattern, a child changing schools. An invitation and never an obligation. It shortens the gap between a change and the adjustment.

5. External calendars | What the household does not control: the school calendar, an activity season, an HOA cycle, a rotating work-travel pattern, a religious calendar. These arrive on someone else’s schedule, often at short notice, through a channel nobody is watching. Capture where the announcements actually land, because household communication is routinely fragmented across several places at once.

section_title: Flags, and the discipline that makes them real
text: Every flag carries a revisit trigger, set at the moment of flagging. A date or a condition. Never a flag without one.

section_title: Flags, and the discipline that makes them real
text: Re-observe every flagged condition at each visit rather than only at its revisit date. A flag records a rate of change as much as a state.

section_title: Flags, and the discipline that makes them real
text: Promote anything degrading faster than its flag assumed, rather than leaving it to its original timing.

section_title: Flags, and the discipline that makes them real
text: Report what was noticed and deliberately left, with the reason and the intended timing. A clean bathroom demonstrates nothing about attention. The caulk in the guest bath starting to go, not urgent, flagged for spring demonstrates it exactly.

section_title: Flags, and the discipline that makes them real
text: A decision that has been researched and then paused is logged with its own revisit trigger, so real research is never lost to time.
Water heater, eight to twelve years. HVAC, fifteen to twenty. Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, ten. A roof by its material’s rated life.
Bleach degrades within about six months even sealed. General cleaning products hold six months to two years. Opened paint, six months to five years.
Stored batteries, including detector batteries, replaced at least annually. Fire extinguishers inspected annually.
Maintenance cycles for every member and pet: dental, medical, vision, grooming, vehicle, renewals. Date, provider and member only, never clinical detail.
Stored value that expires: gift cards, prepaid accounts, subscriptions, use-it-or-lose-it class packages.

House Manager certifications, computed from the date of issue rather than the date of hire. CPR and First Aid lapse at about two years, and an expired card removes someone from solo assignment under WK-STD-022 Section 1. That makes renewal a staffing horizon as much as a compliance one, and it is surfaced a quarter ahead rather than in the week it expires.
Does it change what someone actually does, or does it only produce awareness? A trigger that fires and yields "noted" is a record entry, not a trigger.
Does an existing trigger already own that moment? Two firing on one event are one trigger with two actions and belong together.
Is the cost of missing it higher than the cost of the noise? Density should track consequence, not completeness.
Would a House Manager still trust it a year in? Anything that fired repeatedly and produced no action is a candidate for removal.

section_title: Why this is the retention engine
text: The family that comes home from a funeral to find the guest rooms ready and dinner handled, without having asked, does not churn.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Tier 1 floor under WK-STD-000 Section 1, in full. Nothing in this document is overridden by a household preference, a client request, or an instruction given in the moment.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Every House Manager holds current adult and child CPR and First Aid certification before their first solo visit, and it never lapses. Certification runs about two years, the company pays for it and pays for the time, and renewal is tracked like any other credential.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Adult and child CPR, First Aid, and AED where the training includes it.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Infant CPR additionally for any House Manager assigned to a household with a child under one.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: From a recognized provider. The American Red Cross and the American Heart Association are the usual routes.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: An expired certification means no solo assignment until it is renewed. This is not a paperwork matter.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Renewal is a horizon item under WK-STD-016 Section 6, computed from the issue date and surfaced a quarter ahead. It is never a reminder that arrives in the week a card lapses, because by then it is a scheduling problem rather than a training one.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Well Kept does not provide hands-on personal care. Not bathing, dressing, feeding, or toileting. Not assistance with physical transfer or with walking. Not administering medication. Not once, not a little, not as a favor, and not because someone asked.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Never explain it as a policy you personally disagree with, and never suggest you might bend it.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Report every request the same day. A pattern of requests is a signal the household needs a care referral, and it is one of the most useful things you can surface.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Where a client presses, the conversation moves to the CEO. You are never the person who has to hold that line alone.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Never administer, hand, dispense, prompt by handing, sort, or fill a pill organizer, for any person, in any household, under any circumstance.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Never move a person’s medication except to place it unopened in its documented secure location, per WK-STD-004 and WK-STD-003.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Never read a medication label, count doses, or record what someone takes.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Where a household asks for medication support, that is a care referral and it goes to the CEO the same day.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Note the deliberate asymmetry. WK-STD-009 permits administering pet medication where the Playbook documents it and the House Manager is trained. For people it is never permitted, because the difference is not about care. It is about licensure.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: 1 | Protect yourself | Gas, fire, smoke, electricity, an aggressive animal. You cannot help anyone if you become the second casualty.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: 2 | Call 911 | First, and before calling the client. If you are wondering whether it warrants a call, it warrants a call. Nobody at Well Kept will ever question one.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: 3 | Act within your training | What your CPR and First Aid certification covers, and nothing beyond it.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: 4 | Call the client | Second. Never delay emergency services to reach them first.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: 5 | Call Well Kept | Same day, and within the hour for anything involving a person.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: 6 | Stay | Until help arrives and until you are released. Never leave someone alone after an incident.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: 7 | Write it down | While it is fresh. What, when, what you observed, what you did, who you called.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Do not lift them. Not to a chair, not to their feet, not even if they ask. Lifting can turn a fracture into a worse one and is how the person helping gets hurt too.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Check whether they are responsive and whether they are breathing.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Call 911 for any head strike, any loss of consciousness, any suspected fracture, any bleeding that does not stop, any blood thinner, or any uncertainty at all.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Keep them still and warm. Do not move them unless they are in immediate danger where they are.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Stay with them and keep talking to them.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Call the client, then Well Kept.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Report every fall, including ones where the person got up unaided and insisted they were fine. Especially those.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Call 911 first. Do not wait to see whether it settles and do not wait to reach the client.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: You already know where the epinephrine is kept and whether it is in date, per WK-STD-002 Section 2.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Whether a House Manager may administer an auto-injector is an open question. Lay administration in an emergency is treated differently from administering medication as a service, and the answer must come from counsel rather than from this document. It is settled before the first household with a documented anaphylactic allergy is onboarded, and until then the instruction is to call 911 and get the device to the person or to a family member.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Leave first. Get anyone else out. Call 911 from outside.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Never investigate a gas smell, and never operate a switch or a phone inside a space that smells of gas.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: For water, shut off the supply only if you know where the valve is and can reach it safely. WK-STD-012 is why you already know.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Never re-enter for belongings, pets, or documents.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Any hands-on personal care, in any amount, for any reason.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Lift, transfer, or steady an adult.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Administer, hand, sort, or prompt medication for a person.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Delay emergency services to call the client, to ask permission, or to reach Well Kept.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Act beyond your training because it feels like doing more.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Leave someone alone after an incident.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Downplay or fail to report anything involving a person, however fine they seemed afterward.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Any incident, in full, with what you observed and what you did.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Every fall, without exception.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Every request for personal care or medication support, logged the same day. This is a Channel 2 signal under WK-STD-016 Section 4, not a note. Any request involving transfer, lifting, or medication goes up immediately rather than waiting for a pattern. Two requests of any kind within a month is the threshold at which the CEO opens a care conversation with the family. Adjust these numbers once the pilot has real data.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Anything raising the risk of a fall: a rug, a cord, a dark stair, a missing rail. Each one is flagged with a revisit trigger attached at the moment of flagging, per WK-STD-000 Section 9, and re-observed every visit. In a household with an aging parent or a young child, a fall-risk flag without a revisit date is worse than no flag, because the family now believes it is being watched.

doc_title: Emergency Response and the Personal Care Boundary
text: Certification expiry approaching, yours and anyone you cover for.
Tier 2 floor under WK-STD-000 Section 1 for Sections 2 and 5. Where this standard says stop and refer, no household preference overrides it.

section_title: What you are looking at, and what you are not
text: You assess an environment. You never assess a person. What a room looks like is an observation you are qualified to make. Why it looks that way is not, and it is not your business to conclude.

section_title: What you are looking at, and what you are not
text: Describe conditions, access, and function. Never diagnose, never speculate, and never use clinical words.

section_title: What you are looking at, and what you are not
text: The word hoarding does not appear in a Well Kept report, a Playbook, or a conversation with a client. It is a clinical term, it is not yours to apply, and it damages a relationship instantly.

section_title: What you are looking at, and what you are not
text: Never discuss the household’s condition with anyone outside Well Kept, including other household staff.

section_title: What you are looking at, and what you are not
text: Remember the bereavement register in WK-STD-016. A household in the weeks after a death, a diagnosis, or a job loss can present this way temporarily. That is grief, not chronic disorganization, and the correct response is to absorb friction quietly and propose nothing.
Broadly | What you would see | What we do

Standard | Everything accessible. Doors, stairs and windows clear. Plumbing, electrical and heating working. Detectors functional. Rooms used for their purpose. | Ordinary service and ordinary reset work.

Strained | Systems under pressure. Some rooms crowded, storage overflowing, a surface or two that has become a dumping ground. Everything still functions. | Ordinary service. A reset proposal is appropriate and often exactly right.

The pivot | Access is restricted. A room can no longer be used for its purpose. Hygiene or safety is beginning to be affected. The household is no longer able to correct it between visits. | Stop and refer. Reset work is not appropriate as ordinary scoped service from here up.
Significant | Structural or utility problems. Pest activity. Rooms unusable. Conditions affecting health. | Refer, and the safety conditions in Section 3 govern what we do meanwhile.
Severe | Conditions that are not habitable. Utilities not working. Biohazard. | Stop work. This is not a cleaning or organizing problem.

Maintenance capacity is the leading indicator. Whether a household can hold a reset area between visits tells you more than any single photograph. Three consecutive visits where a previously reset area has not been held is the threshold at which this is raised, before the pivot is reached. Adjust the number once the pilot has real data.

Every environmental finding carries a revisit trigger, per WK-STD-000 Section 9, and is re-observed each visit rather than at the review. A condition worsening faster than its flag assumed is promoted.

Watch the precipitants. Most of what sends a household in this direction is already in the life-events register in WK-STD-016 Section 2: a bereavement, a diagnosis, a job loss, a move, retirement, an empty nest. When one of those fires, the household is more vulnerable for the months that follow and the observation matters more.
Record improvement with the same discipline as decline. A household recovering is the single most useful thing this standard produces and it is the one nobody thinks to write down.

section_title: Conditions that stop work regardless of level
text: Blocked egress. If a path to an exit cannot be cleared safely, work stops until it can.

section_title: Conditions that stop work regardless of level
text: Non-functioning utilities: no working water, heat, or electricity in a lived-in space.

section_title: Conditions that stop work regardless of level
text: Active pest infestation, or rodent droppings, which are never disturbed. WK-STD-012 governs.

section_title: Conditions that stop work regardless of level
text: Any biohazard, including human or animal waste beyond an ordinary accident.

section_title: Conditions that stop work regardless of level
text: Structural concerns: floors that flex, ceilings that sag, anything stacked to a height that could fall.

section_title: Conditions that stop work regardless of level
text: Air that is difficult to breathe, or a strong ammonia or mold smell.
Report what you observed, in environmental language, with photographs where consent permits.
Never raise it with the client yourself unless you have been asked to.
Never express surprise, distaste, or concern in the moment. A household in this situation has usually been judged before and is expecting it again.
Continue treating the household exactly as you treat every other. The service does not become colder because the house is harder.
Discard, move, or consolidate belongings to make progress, however obviously worthless they appear.
Push a household to part with anything.
Use clinical language, in speech or in writing.
Photograph the condition without consent, or share any photograph beyond Well Kept and the client.
Take on reset work above the pivot because the household asked and it seemed unkind to decline.
Work in conditions listed in Section 3.
Treat a household differently in tone, warmth, or care because of what you have seen.
Environmental observations only, in plain descriptive language.
Access and safety conditions, and anything from Section 3.
Change over time, in either direction. Improvement matters as much as decline and is worth recording.
Whether the household is able to maintain between visits, which is the leading indicator and carries the threshold in Section 2.
Never a conclusion about why.
